pages.title: Introduction
pages.content:
Adam (pbuh) was the first human being to be created, and the first prophet who served as a guide and example for mankind. We learn his story from the Holy Qur’an. Based on the Holy Qur’an, the creation of Adam (pbuh) is not like the creation of other humans. He was created from clay without parents, as a miraculous sign of Allah’s unlimited power. The story of Adam (pbuh) is told in several chapters (surahs) of the Holy Qur’an. These are Surah Baqarah, Surah Al-Imran, Surah A’raf, Surah Hijr, Surah Isra, Surah Kahf, Surah Taha, and Surah Sad. In these surahs, Satan is portrayed as a rebel against Allah’s command but also as a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah.

Adam (pbuh)’s tale is not symbolic or imaginary, but it is an original factual tale with historical correctness and reality, from which we can take many lessons and morals. It also includes the Unseen (al-ghayb), and this makes the story fabulous. The tale gives us a unique and deeply philosophical understanding of life. It clearly appears that human beings' earthly life is the scene of a division and contrast between good and evil as opposed to each other.

vocabulary.definition: Beyond ordinary natural processes through divine power.
Remarkable or extraordinary in character.
Concerned with basic questions of knowledge and existence.
The hidden reality that the human senses cannot perceive.
A clear difference between opposing ideas.

hotspots.title: The First Prophet
hotspots.description: Adam (pbuh) was the first human being and the first prophet, a guide and example for mankind.

hotspots.title: Good Versus Evil
hotspots.description: Human life on Earth is shown as a scene where good and evil stand against each other.

exercises.title: What Kind of Tale?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that matches the writer’s position in Chapter 1.
exercises.question: How does the writer describe the nature of Adam’s tale?
options: as a symbolic story that teaches morals through imagined events
as a factual tale with historical reality that also includes the Unseen
as a philosophical theory about good and evil rather than a real event
exercises.explanation: The second paragraph says the tale “is not symbolic or imaginary, but it is an original factual tale with historical correctness and reality”, and adds that “it also includes the Unseen (al-ghayb)”.

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer rejects a symbolic reading and calls the tale factual, while noting that it includes the Unseen.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first sentence of the second paragraph again. Look at the “not …, but …” structure: Which reading does the writer reject, and which one does he choose?

languageFocusExercises.title: Source, Focus and Correction
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort each part of the Chapter 1 introduction by what it does.
languageFocusExercises.question: Does it name the source, put the topic first, or correct an idea?

dragDropGroups.group: Names the source of the account
items: We learn his story from the Holy Qur’an.
Based on the Holy Qur’an, …

dragDropGroups.group: Puts the person or thing affected first (passive)
items: He was created from clay without parents
The story of Adam (pbuh) is told in several chapters (surahs) of the Holy Qur’an.
Satan is portrayed as a rebel against Allah’s command

dragDropGroups.group: Rejects or narrows one idea in favor of another
items: a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah
not symbolic or imaginary, but it is an original factual tale

Names the source of the account: We learn his story from the Holy Qur’an.
Puts the person or thing affected first: He was created from clay without parents
The story of Adam (pbuh) is told in several chapters (surahs) of the Holy Qur’an.
Satan is portrayed as a rebel against Allah’s command
Rejects or narrows one idea in favor of: a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah
not symbolic or imaginary, but it is an original factual tale

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A careful introduction makes three choices visible. It names where its information comes from (“We learn his story from …”, “Based on …”). It uses the passive (be + past participle) to keep the topic, Adam or his story or Satan, at the front of the sentence because who does the telling or portraying is already known or less important. And it refines ideas: “not X, but Y” rejects one reading and replaces it, while “X rather than Y” narrows the focus to the more accurate option.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated naming a source, choosing the sentence focus with the passive, and correcting or narrowing an idea.
feedback.incorrect: Ask three questions: Does it say where the story comes from? Does it use be + past participle? Does it reject or narrow an idea? Then check both paragraphs of Chapter 1.

languageFocusExercises.title: Same Meaning, Different Framing
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines about Adam’s story?

transformItems.source: Adam (pbuh)’s tale is not symbolic or imaginary, but it is an original factual tale with historical correctness and reality …
transformItems.frame: Adam (pbuh)’s tale is an original factual tale [blank] symbolic or imaginary.

transformItems.source: The story of Adam (pbuh) is told in several chapters (surahs) of the Holy Qur’an.
transformItems.frame: The Holy Qur’an [blank] the story of Adam (pbuh) in several chapters (surahs).

transformItems.source: In these surahs, Satan is portrayed as a rebel against Allah’s command …
transformItems.frame: These surahs [blank] Satan as a rebel against Allah’s command.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not symbolic …, but … factual” and “a factual tale rather than a symbolic one” make the same correction; the first rejects before it replaces, the second puts the accepted idea first. The active versions (“The Holy Qur’an tells …”, “These surahs portray …”) are correct, but they move the source to the front. The chapter prefers the passive because its paragraph is about Adam’s story and about Satan, so those stay in subject position.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the claim while changing the framing.
feedback.incorrect: For item 1, use a phrase that puts the accepted idea first and the rejected one after it. For items 2 and 3, make the Qur’an or the surahs the subject and use a present simple verb.

languageFocusExercises.title: Keep the Writer’s Distinction
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose the summary with the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: “In these surahs, Satan is portrayed as a rebel against Allah’s command but also as a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah.” Which summary keeps this meaning?
options: Satan is shown as a rival and enemy of both Allah and Adam in equal measure.
Satan disobeys Allah’s command, but he is shown as the rival and enemy of Adam, not of Allah.
Satan is shown only as Adam’s enemy; the surahs do not mention any disobedience.
Satan is shown as Allah’s rival rather than Adam’s enemy.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The sentence makes two claims. “A rebel against Allah’s command” describes disobedience. “A rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah” narrows the rivalry: The enemy he competes with is Adam, not Allah. A good summary keeps both claims and does not turn “rather than” into “and”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The summary keeps the rebellion and keeps the rivalry focused on Adam.
feedback.incorrect: Look closely at “rather than Allah” at the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 1. Whose rival is Satan?

languageFocusExercises.title: A Story and Its Source
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write 6–8 sentences about a story from history that you know, and say where it comes from.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you tell a story and name its source?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response identifies its source, chooses information focus deliberately and uses contrast to refine meaning rather than simply list facts.

feedback.correct: Keep source, focus and certainty visible throughout the paragraph.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Name your source: “According to …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: According to his travel book, the Rihla, Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. Based on the same book, his journeys lasted almost thirty years.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Put the book or event first: “It was written by …”
discussionPrompts.example: The book was not written by Ibn Battuta’s own hand. It was dictated to a scholar called Ibn Juzayy after the traveler returned to Morocco.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Correct an idea: “It is … rather than …”
discussionPrompts.example: So the Rihla is a remembered account rather than a daily diary. It is not only an adventure story. It is, rather, a rich source about life in many lands.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — End with a contrast: “Many details …. However, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Many details in the book are confirmed by other sources. However, some dates and routes are less certain, so historians read those parts with more care.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What was Adam (pbuh) created from?
options: from fire
from light
from clay without parents
beforeYouRead.quote: He was created from clay without parents

iCan: I can say where the story of Adam (pbuh) comes from and why it is special.
I can name my source and correct an idea with “rather”.
I can write a short paragraph about an account I know and its source.

pages.title: The Creation of Adam
pages.content:
The material from which Adam (pbuh) was created is expressed in various verses using different terms: earth (turab), water (ma’), clay (tin), etc. These different expressions are used to describe both the composition and the various stages of mud, which is a mixture of water and soil. As an example, Surah Sad, verse 71, informs that Allah created Adam (pbuh) out of clay, which is a humble material: “Your Lord said to the angels, ‘I am creating a human being from clay.’”

Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) also said: “Allah created Adam (pbuh) from a handful of dust taken from different lands, so the children of Adam (pbuh) have been created according to the composition of the land. Therefore, from mankind we have white, red, black, and yellow ones; we have good and evil, ease and sorrow, and what comes in between them.” (see Abu Dawud, Sunnah 16; Tirmidhi, Tafsir 2/1) So, in essence, people are from the same soil and they have no superiority over one another due to the difference in their colors.

It is clear that Adam (pbuh) did not evolve from any other living being, but was created from the earth and was the first ancestor of a completely separate species of human being. He was given the necessary spiritual, moral, mental, and psychological abilities.

vocabulary.definition: The materials or elements that form something.
A whole formed by combining different substances.
The state of being regarded as higher or better.
A person from whom later generations descend.
A distinct biological group of living beings.

hotspots.title: Shared Human Origin
hotspots.description: All people come from the same soil, so no color makes anyone superior to another.

hotspots.title: Human Capacities
hotspots.description: Adam (pbuh) was given the spiritual, moral, mental and psychological abilities he needed.

exercises.title: Which Source Says What?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 2.
exercises.question: In Chapter 2, the information that people have different colors comes from the verse of Surah Sad.
exercises.explanation: The verse of Surah Sad (71) says only that Allah created a human being “from clay”. The different colors (“white, red, black, and yellow”) come from the saying of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) about the handful of dust. From this hadith the writer concludes that people “have no superiority over one another due to the difference in their colors.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The verse is about clay; the colors come from the hadith, and the writer builds his conclusion on it.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the two sources. Read the verse at the end of the first paragraph, then the saying at the start of the second paragraph. Which one lists colors?

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Which” Add?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 2. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “These different expressions are used to describe both the composition and the various stages of mud, which is a mixture of water and soil.” What does “which is a mixture of water and soil” do?
options: It tells us which kind of mud is meant, as opposed to other kinds of mud.
It gives the reason why the verses use different expressions.
It adds a short definition of “mud” for the reader; the sentence is complete without it.
It introduces an example taken from a verse.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A comma before “which” marks a non-defining relative clause: It adds extra information about a noun that is already clear. Here it defines “mud” for readers who may not know how the terms earth, water and clay fit together. Compare the first sentence of the chapter, “The material from which Adam (pbuh) was created …”: there is no comma because the clause is needed to say which material is meant.

feedback.correct: Correct. The comma shows extra, defining information about a word that is already clear.
feedback.incorrect: Remove the clause and read the sentence again: Is anything missing? Then compare it with the first sentence of Chapter 2, which has no comma.

languageFocusExercises.title: Where Adam Came From
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say how Adam was created?

transformItems.source: The material from which Adam (pbuh) was created is expressed in various verses using different terms …
transformItems.frame: The material [blank] is expressed in various verses using different terms.

transformItems.source: … Surah Sad, verse 71, informs that Allah created Adam (pbuh) out of clay, which is a humble material …
transformItems.frame: … Surah Sad, verse 71, informs that Adam (pbuh) [blank] out of clay by Allah.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “The material from which Adam was created” is formal: The preposition goes before “which”. In less formal English the preposition moves to the end (“the material which/that Adam was created from”), and “which/that” can be left out. In item 2 the passive “Adam was created … by Allah” makes Adam the subject, which suits a chapter whose topic is Adam’s creation.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the meaning while changing the structure.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: put “from” at the end of the relative clause. Item 2: use was + past participle because “by Allah” is already in the sentence.

languageFocusExercises.title: Example, Conclusion, Correction
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 2 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word gives an example, which sums up, and which corrects?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: [blank], Surah Sad, verse 71, informs that Allah created Adam (pbuh) out of clay, which is a humble material … [blank], in essence, people are from the same soil and they have no superiority over one another due to the difference in their colors. It is clear that Adam (pbuh) did not evolve from any other living being, [blank] was created from the earth …
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “As an example” moves from the general statement about different terms to one specific verse. “So, in essence” draws a conclusion from the hadith: People come from the same soil, so color gives no one superiority. “did not …, but was …” rejects one idea (evolution from another being) and replaces it with the chapter’s claim.

feedback.correct: Correct. You linked the general point, the example, the conclusion and the correction.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each gap does: Introduce a specific case, sum up what follows from the hadith, or replace a rejected idea. Then check the order of the three paragraphs in Chapter 2.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build an Evidence-to-Conclusion Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write 6–8 sentences to explain how something works, with an example and a conclusion.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you explain an idea and end with a clear conclusion?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response introduces the concept, clarifies the descriptions, gives evidence and signals a justified conclusion.

feedback.correct: Keep each sentence connected to the evidence–conclusion chain.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what it is: “… is the process that …”
discussionPrompts.example: The water cycle is the process that moves water between the sea, the air and the land. Water that falls as rain finally returns to the rivers and the sea.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what happens to it: “… is heated / carried by …”
discussionPrompts.example: Every day, huge amounts of sea water are heated by the sun and turned into vapour. This vapour is then carried by the wind over the land.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give an example: “For example, …”
discussionPrompts.example: For example, the rain that falls on a mountain may once have been part of the ocean. A cloud, for instance, is simply vapour that has cooled into tiny drops.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — End with a conclusion: “Therefore, …”
discussionPrompts.example: The same water is used again and again in different forms. Therefore, it makes sense to call it one cycle and not many separate events.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What does the chapter say about people of different colors?
options: They are all from the same soil.
They come from different first parents.
Some colors are better than others.
beforeYouRead.quote: people are from the same soil and they have no superiority over one another due to the difference in their colors

iCan: I can explain what the chapter says about clay and our shared origin.
I can define a word and give an example before a conclusion.
I can explain an idea step by step and end with “therefore”.

pages.title: The Vicegerent & The Gift of Knowledge
pages.content:
To be a representative, Adam (pbuh) needed some extraordinary qualities. Allah breathed His own spirit into Adam (pbuh) (see Sad: 72). Also, he had to be taught by Allah. Breathing Allah’s spirit into Adam (pbuh) shows the value that Allah gave him. It also means giving Adam (pbuh) life and the beginning of human existence. This also distinguishes Adam (pbuh) from the rest of the creatures. Then, He (Allah) taught him all the names.

“And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said, ‘Tell Me the names of these, if you are sincere.’ They said, ‘Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. It is You who are the Knowledgeable, the Wise.’ He said, ‘O Adam, tell them their names.’ And when he (Adam) told them their names, He said, ‘Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and that I know what you reveal and what you conceal?’” (Baqarah: 31-33)

The statement “Allah taught Adam (pbuh) all the names” points to the breadth of Adam (pbuh)’s knowledge. The names taught to Adam (pbuh) could be the fundamental knowledge of being human, thinking, forming logical judgments, and producing civilization and culture. The knowledge that was given to Adam (pbuh) means the beginning of the skill for learning and speaking language and using intelligence. The names refer to the fact that knowledge is the basis of science, technology, and culture.

vocabulary.definition: A person entrusted with responsibility on behalf of another.
Very unusual or remarkable.
Basic and essential to a larger structure.
An organized society with developed culture and knowledge.
The ability to learn, reason, and use knowledge.

hotspots.title: Taught All the Names
hotspots.description: Allah taught Adam (pbuh) all the names, which set him apart from the rest of creation.

hotspots.title: Knowledge and Civilization
hotspots.description: Language and reasoning are linked with civilization and culture.

matchingHeadings.right: What it shows or tells us

exercises.title: Event and Meaning
exercises.instructions: Match each part of Chapter 3 with what the chapter says about it.
exercises.question: What does the chapter draw from each part of the account?

matchingPairs.left: Allah breathed His spirit into Adam
matchingPairs.right: the value Allah gave him, which sets him apart from other creatures

matchingPairs.left: The word “all” in “all the names”
matchingPairs.right: how broad Adam’s understanding was

matchingPairs.left: The angels’ reply to Allah
matchingPairs.right: they know only what Allah has taught them

correctAnswer.Allah breathed His spirit into Adam: the value Allah gave him, which sets him apart from other creatures
correctAnswer.The angels’ reply to Allah: they know only what Allah has taught them

exercises.explanation: The first paragraph says breathing the spirit “shows the value that Allah gave him” and “distinguishes Adam (pbuh) from the rest of the creatures”. The last paragraph says “all the names” “points to the breadth of Adam (pbuh)’s knowledge”. In the verse the angels say, “We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.”

feedback.correct: Well done. You separated what happened from what the writer says it shows.
feedback.incorrect: Check each part in its place: The spirit in the first paragraph, the angels’ words in the verse, and “all the names” in the last paragraph. What does the text say each one shows?

languageFocusExercises.title: Strong Claim or Careful Suggestion?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the parts of Chapter 3: a sure meaning or a possible one?
languageFocusExercises.question: How sure is the writer about each meaning?

dragDropGroups.group: States the meaning directly
items: Breathing Allah’s spirit into Adam (pbuh) shows the value that Allah gave him.
It also means giving Adam (pbuh) life and the beginning of human existence.
The names refer to the fact that knowledge is the basis of science, technology, and culture.

dragDropGroups.group: Suggests a possible or partial meaning
items: The statement “Allah taught Adam (pbuh) all the names” points to the breadth of Adam (pbuh)’s knowledge.
… could be the fundamental knowledge of being human, thinking, forming logical judgments …

States the meaning directly: Breathing Allah’s spirit into Adam (pbuh) shows the value that Allah gave him.
It also means giving Adam (pbuh) life and the beginning of human existence.
The names refer to the fact that knowledge is the basis of science, technology, and culture.
Suggests a possible or partial meaning: The statement “Allah taught Adam (pbuh) all the names” points to the breadth of Adam (pbuh)’s knowledge.
… could be the fundamental knowledge of being human, thinking, forming logical judgments …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Verbs such as “shows”, “means” and “refer to” present an interpretation as the writer’s direct reading. “Points to” is weaker: The wording indicates something without spelling it out. “Could be” is weaker still: It offers one possible interpretation, not a certain identification. Good B2 readers notice these differences and keep them when they report the text.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated direct statements of meaning from careful suggestions.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb in each part. Does it state a meaning (shows, means, refer to) or only suggest one (points to, could be)? Check the first and last paragraphs of Chapter 3.

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Was Taught?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about Adam being taught?

errorItems.sentence: Also, he had to taught by Allah.
options: had to be teach
had to be taught
had to teaching

errorItems.sentence: The names teaching to Adam (pbuh) could be the fundamental knowledge of being human, …
options: taught
teached
teach

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Adam receives the teaching, so the verb must be passive. After a modal of necessity, the passive is had to + be + past participle: “he had to be taught by Allah”. After a noun, a past participle can stand for a full passive relative clause: “the names taught to Adam” = “the names which were taught to Adam”. An -ing form would wrongly make the names do the teaching.

feedback.correct: Well done. Both sentences now show that Adam receives the teaching.
feedback.incorrect: Ask who does the teaching and who receives it. The receiver needs a passive form: be + past participle, or a past participle alone after a noun. Check the first and third paragraphs of Chapter 3.

languageFocusExercises.title: Report the Stance Accurately
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the summary of Chapter 3’s last paragraph that is just as sure as the writer.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which summary is not stronger or weaker than the writer’s words?
options: The chapter proves that the names were a complete list of every scientific fact.
The chapter states that the names are certainly the knowledge of thinking and culture, and nothing else.
The chapter suggests that the names may stand for basic human knowledge, such as thinking and producing culture, and links knowledge with science and culture.
The chapter says that it is impossible to know anything about the meaning of the names.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The writer uses “could be” for the exact content of the names, so a summary needs a similar hedge (may, might, suggests). Options that say “proves” or “certainly” overclaim; the option that says nothing can be known underclaims because the writer does offer an interpretation.

feedback.correct: Correct. The summary keeps the writer’s careful “could be” stance.
feedback.incorrect: Find “could be” in the last paragraph of Chapter 3. Which summary is neither stronger nor weaker than that?

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Qualified Interpretation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write 7–9 sentences about some evidence and what it might mean.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you show how sure you are about what evidence means?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response moves from evidence to interpretation while making stronger and weaker claims visibly different.

feedback.correct: Keep each interpretation proportional to the evidence that supports it.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give the evidence: “This term, …”
discussionPrompts.example: This term, the school library has been full every lunchtime, and twenty new students have borrowed books.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what it shows: “The … shows that …”
discussionPrompts.example: The borrowing list shows that interest in reading has grown this term.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Make a careful point: “… points to …”
discussionPrompts.example: The long waiting list for the new science books points to a special interest in science.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — End with a possibility: “This could / may be because …”
discussionPrompts.example: This could be because of the new science club, but it may also simply be because the library is warm in winter.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: According to the writer, what is knowledge the basis of?
options: wealth and power
war and peace
science, technology and culture
beforeYouRead.quote: knowledge is the basis of science, technology, and culture

iCan: I can explain what the gift of the names means.
I can show how sure I am with “shows”, “points to” and “may”.
I can give a careful reading of some evidence.

pages.title: Angels’ Prostration & Iblis’s Arrogance
pages.content:
The reason why Adam (pbuh) and his offspring are considered higher and more valuable than other beings (see Isra: 70) is because of the power of knowledge that Allah gave them.

However, in the Qur’an, Allah mentions another type of knowledge, which is the revelation (wahy) (see Nisa: 163-165). He delivers it to mankind through the prophets. It is clear that human beings need both types of knowledge. These two types of knowledge are not alternatives to each other, but rather they complete one another. One is necessary for mankind to maintain his worldly life, and revelation is essential to understand his role, duty, and the order established by Allah. Having such honor and privilege of knowledge required even the angels to prostrate themselves before Adam (pbuh). Here, the tale reaches its rising action: ‘And We said to the angels, “Bow down to (prostrate) Adam.” They bowed down, except for Satan. He refused, was arrogant, and was one of the disbelievers.’ (Baqarah: 34) ‘Except for Satan. He was too proud, and one of the faithless.’ (Sad: 74) He said, ‘O Satan, what prevented you from prostrating before what I created with My own hands? Are you too proud, or were you one of the exalted?’ (Sad: 75) He (Satan) said, ‘I am better than he (Adam); You created me from fire, and You created him from clay.’ (Sad: 76)

vocabulary.definition: A person’s children and later descendants.
Divine knowledge communicated through prophets.
Absolutely necessary for an important purpose.
A special honor or advantage.
Showing an exaggerated sense of superiority.

hotspots.title: Two Forms of Knowledge
hotspots.description: Worldly knowledge and revelation complete each other.

hotspots.title: Refusing to Bow Down
hotspots.description: Iblis refused to prostrate, claiming that his origin of fire was better than Adam’s (pbuh) clay.

exercises.title: Two Kinds of Knowledge
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer supported by Chapter 4.
exercises.question: According to the chapter, what does revelation help people understand?
options: how to maintain their life in this world
the names of all things on Earth
their role, their duty and the order established by Allah
why Satan was created from fire
exercises.explanation: The chapter gives each kind of knowledge a different job: One “is necessary for mankind to maintain his worldly life, and revelation is essential to understand his role, duty, and the order established by Allah.” That is why the two “complete one another”.

feedback.correct: Right. Revelation explains role, duty and divine order, while the other knowledge supports worldly life.
feedback.incorrect: Find the sentence in the second paragraph that begins “One is necessary for mankind …”. It gives one job to each kind of knowledge. Which job belongs to revelation?

languageFocusExercises.title: Either/Or or Both?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 4. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: The writer presents worldly knowledge and revelation as alternatives: A person needs one or the other.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not alternatives …, but rather they complete one another” rejects an either/or reading and replaces it with a both/and reading. The rest of the paragraph gives each type of knowledge its own job, one for worldly life and one for understanding role and duty, so the two are complementary, not competing.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Not … but rather …” rejects the idea of alternatives.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the word “not” before “alternatives” and at what comes after “but rather”. Then read the next sentence in Chapter 4.

languageFocusExercises.title: What We Need to Do
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: After “require someone” and “necessary for someone”: “to” + verb or -ing?

errorItems.sentence: Having such honor and privilege of knowledge required even the angels prostrating themselves before Adam (pbuh).
options: prostrate
to prostrate
for prostrating

errorItems.sentence: One is necessary for mankind maintaining his worldly life, and revelation is essential to understand his role, duty, and the order established by Allah.
options: to maintain
maintain
to maintaining

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Require” is followed by a person and a to-infinitive: require someone to do something. “Necessary” and “essential” take for + person + to-infinitive: Necessary for someone to do something. The to-infinitive states what the knowledge makes possible or required.

languageFocusExercises.title: Introduce the Second Kind of Knowledge

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “However” shifts from the knowledge Allah gave Adam to a different type. “Which is the revelation” identifies that type (which for a thing, not who). “Through the prophets” names the channel. “Both types” includes the two kinds together; “either” would suggest a choice between them, the reading the chapter rejects.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Complementarity Argument

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say how they differ: “A … gives …. However, a …”

pages.title: Angels’ Prostration & Iblis’s Arrogance — Part II
pages.content:
Angels admitted their inability and realized that Adam (pbuh) was the creature who knew what they did not know and that his capacity to learn was his most honorable quality. Adam (pbuh)’s knowledge included knowledge of the Creator, which is faith or Islam, as well as the knowledge he would need to inhabit and master the earth. All kinds of worldly knowledge are included in this. The prostration of angels to Adam (pbuh) is not a prostration of worship because such prostration is solely to and for Allah. Angels’ prostration means obedience to Allah to show respect and admiration to Adam (pbuh) because the unique knowledge given to Adam (pbuh) is different from the knowledge of the angels that never changes.

On the other hand, Iblis’ arrogance came from his belief that his origin was superior to Adam (pbuh)’s. Satan’s—in other words, Iblis’—hidden arrogance came to the surface when Adam (pbuh) appeared on the scene. He underlines his superiority because of the material from which he was created, yet Adam (pbuh)’s humble origin shows that Allah does not focus on origins, that is, race, color, or ethnicity, since all humans ultimately originate from dried mud.

vocabulary.definition: The condition of being unable to do something.
Willing compliance with a command or authority.
Respect and approval for someone’s qualities.
Simple and low in status; not grand or important.
Identity linked to shared cultural or ancestral background.

exercises.title: Answering Iblis
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer supported by Chapter 5.
exercises.question: Iblis claims he is better because of the material he was created from. What does the writer use to answer this claim?
options: the angels’ knowledge, which never changes
Adam’s humble origin, which shows that Allah does not focus on origins
the angels’ prostration, which was an act of worship
Adam’s wish to live forever in Paradise
exercises.explanation: At the end of the chapter the writer says Iblis “underlines his superiority because of the material from which he was created, yet Adam (pbuh)’s humble origin shows that Allah does not focus on origins, that is, race, color, or ethnicity, since all humans ultimately originate from dried mud.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer turns Adam’s humble origin into evidence that origin, race and color do not decide a person’s value.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of the chapter. After the word “yet”, what does the writer set against Iblis’s claim?

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does Each Clarification Explain?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 5 with what it explains.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The three markers are close in meaning but do different jobs here. “Which is …” defines the phrase just before it. “In other words” restates a name so the reader can follow who is meant. “That is” makes a broad word (origins) concrete. A separate sentence (“All kinds of … are included in this”) widens the scope of a category.

feedback.correct: Correct. You linked each clarification to the word or idea it explains.
feedback.incorrect: Find each expression in Chapter 5 and read the words just before it. What is being defined, renamed, listed or widened?

languageFocusExercises.title: Recombine Cause and Contrast
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we join these ideas from Chapter 5?

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “X, yet Y” and “Although X, Y” express the same contrast, but “although” goes before the point that is conceded. “Y because X” and “X; therefore, Y” express the same logic in opposite orders: “because” introduces the cause, “therefore” introduces the result.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the logic while changing the linker and the order.

languageFocusExercises.title: Challenge a Weak Criterion

pages.title: The Command to Paradise
pages.content:
Allah said: “O Mankind! Be respectful to your Lord, Who created you from a single person (Adam) and from Him (Adam) He created his wife (Eve), and from them both He created many men and women.” (Nisa: 1)

Adam (pbuh) was now in Paradise and not alone; he had his wife with him.

Allah spoke to Adam (pbuh) in A’raf, verse 19: “And you, Adam, inhabit the Garden, you and your wife, and eat whatever you wish; but do not approach this tree, for fear that you become wrongdoers.”

The tale went on. While Satan reached the point of no return by challenging his Creator, Adam (pbuh) took a path completely different from him. Surah A’raf, verses 16-17: “Satan said, ‘Because You have put me in error, I will surely sit in wait for them (Adam’s children) on Your Straight Path. Then I will come to them from before them, and from behind them, and from their right, and from their left; and you will not find most of them grateful to You.’”

The tale is unfolding through the verses 77-82 in Surah Sad: Allah said, “Then get out of here! You (Satan) are an outcast! And My curse will be upon you until the Day of Judgment.” He said, “Lord, allow me until the Day they are raised up.” He said, “You are one of those allowed, until the Day of the Time Appointed.” He said, “By Your majesty, I will deceive them all.”

vocabulary.definition: Showing honor and proper regard; here, mindful of one’s duty to Allah.
To live in or occupy a place.
People who violate a moral or religious command.
Someone rejected and excluded from a group.
Feeling or showing thanks for what one has been given.

hotspots.description: Adam (pbuh) and his wife were allowed to live in the Garden and eat freely, but not to approach one tree.

exercises.title: From Challenge to Threat
exercises.instructions: Put the steps of Satan’s story in Chapter 6 in order.
exercises.question: How does Satan move from challenging his Creator to declaring his plan?

sequencingItems.text: Allah orders him to get out and calls him an outcast.
Satan asks for time until the Day people are raised up.
Allah gives him time until the Day of the Time Appointed.
Satan swears by Allah’s majesty that he will deceive them all.

exercises.explanation: The chapter says Satan “reached the point of no return by challenging his Creator”. The verses of Surah Sad (77–82) then show the steps: Allah expels and curses him, Satan asks to be allowed time, Allah grants it, and Satan swears, “By Your majesty, I will deceive them all.”

feedback.correct: Well done. Satan’s threat comes only after he is expelled and given time.
feedback.incorrect: Follow the conversation in the verses of Surah Sad at the end of the chapter: Who speaks first, what is asked for, and what is given?

languageFocusExercises.title: Freedom, Limit and Request
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each line from the verses in Chapter 6 with what it does.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is allowed, what is forbidden, and what is asked for?

matchingPairs.left: inhabit the Garden, you and your wife
matchingPairs.right: tells them where to live

matchingPairs.left: eat whatever you wish
matchingPairs.right: gives wide freedom of choice

matchingPairs.left: do not approach this tree
matchingPairs.right: forbids one thing

matchingPairs.left: for fear that you become wrongdoers
matchingPairs.right: warns what will follow disobedience

matchingPairs.left: Lord, allow me until the Day they are raised up.
matchingPairs.right: asks for more time

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The imperative can command, permit or forbid. “Inhabit” and “eat whatever you wish” open a wide space of freedom; “do not approach” sets a single limit inside it, and “for fear that …” gives the reason for that limit. Satan’s “allow me until …” is a different speech act: A request for permission with a time limit.

feedback.correct: Correct. You identified permission, prohibition, warning and request.
feedback.incorrect: Read A’raf 19 and the verses from Surah Sad again in Chapter 6. Which line opens freedom, which one limits it, which one explains the limit, and who asks for something?

languageFocusExercises.title: Two Paths in One Sentence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “While” here means “whereas”: it sets two different paths side by side. It can start the sentence or join the second clause. “By challenging” shows the means by which Satan reached the point of no return; a full clause can express this as a cause or a time (“because / when he challenged …”).

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the contrast and the link between action and result.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: you need a word that contrasts two paths. Item 2: you need a linker plus a subject because “challenged” is already given.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Will” Express Here?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read Satan’s words quoted in Chapter 6. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: In “I will surely sit in wait for them … on Your Straight Path” and “By Your majesty, I will deceive them all”, what does “will” express?
options: a prediction based on something the speaker can already see
an offer to help the people he is talking about
a firm intention that the speaker declares, even with an oath
a habit that the speaker had in the past
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Will” is not only a neutral future. With “surely” and the oath “By Your majesty”, it states determination: The speaker announces what he intends to do. Repeating it (“I will surely sit …”, “I will come …”, “I will deceive …”) makes the threat sound deliberate and continuous.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Will” here declares a firm intention.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the words around “will”: “surely” and “By Your majesty”. Is the speaker predicting, offering, or declaring what he is determined to do?

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Contrast with Boundaries and Intentions
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 7–9 sentences about two people who choose very different paths.
languageFocusExercises.question: How are the two paths different?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response makes the boundary clear, establishes the contrast early, develops each path logically, and uses future forms to communicate intention or commitment rather than merely future time.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what is allowed or not: “… are allowed to …, but …”

pages.title: The Whisper of Deception
pages.content:
Adam (pbuh) and Eve understood that they were forbidden to eat the fruit of that tree. Adam (pbuh) was, however, a human being, and man tends to forget. His heart changes, and his determination weakens. On the other hand, Satan would seek a way to remove Adam (pbuh) from mercy because he thought of Adam (pbuh) as the cause of his expulsion from Allah’s mercy. He took advantage of Adam (pbuh)’s humanity to manipulate him. He started to whisper to them day after day, trying to persuade both:

“But Satan whispered to them (Adam and Eve), to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said, ‘Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree, lest you become angels, or become immortals.’” (A’raf: 20) And he swore to them, “I am a sincere advisor to you.” (A’raf: 21) Upon Satan’s promise that he was their true friend, Adam (pbuh) started to ask himself: “What will happen if I eat from this tree? It might truly be the Tree of Immortality.” His dream was to live forever in the pure innocence of Paradise. Years went by, and Adam (pbuh) and Eve were preoccupied with thoughts of that tree. Then one day, they decided to eat of its fruit. They forgot that Allah had warned them not to approach it and that Iblis was their bitter enemy. Adam (pbuh) stretched out his hand, picked one of the fruits, and offered it to Eve. They both ate of the forbidden tree. As soon as Adam (pbuh) had finished eating, he felt his heart tighten and fill with pain, sadness, and shame. The surrounding atmosphere changed, and the internal harmony ceased.

vocabulary.definition: Firmness of purpose in following a decision.
Spoke very softly; here, secretly put tempting ideas into someone’s mind.
Beings believed to live forever.
Honest and genuine in intention.
Thinking about something so much that there is little room for anything else.

hotspots.title: Weakening Determination
hotspots.description: Satan used human forgetfulness, whispering to Adam (pbuh) and Eve day after day.

hotspots.title: The Forbidden Tree
hotspots.description: Adam (pbuh) and Eve eventually ate from the tree they had been warned about.

exercises.title: Satan’s Motive
exercises.instructions: Choose the reason given in Chapter 7.
exercises.question: Why did Satan want to remove Adam from Allah’s mercy?
options: He wanted to live forever in Paradise himself.
He saw Adam as the cause of his own expulsion from Allah’s mercy.
Adam had been given knowledge that Satan did not have.
exercises.explanation: The first paragraph says Satan “would seek a way to remove Adam (pbuh) from mercy because he thought of Adam (pbuh) as the cause of his expulsion from Allah’s mercy.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The text gives Satan’s motive with “because”: he blamed Adam for his own expulsion.
feedback.incorrect: Look in the first paragraph for the sentence about Satan that contains “because”. What did Satan think about Adam?

languageFocusExercises.title: People in General or This Story?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the parts of Chapter 7: true of all people, or one event?
languageFocusExercises.question: Is it true of people in general, or only of this story?

One event in this story: Satan took advantage of Adam (pbuh)’s humanity to manipulate him.
Then one day, they decided to eat of its fruit.
They both ate of the forbidden tree.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: In a past-tense story, a sudden present simple (“man tends to forget”, “His heart changes”, “his determination weakens”) signals a general truth: What is true of human beings at any time. The past simple returns to particular events. The writer uses the general truth to explain why the particular events could happen.

feedback.correct: Correct. The present simple gives the general truth; the past simple tells the events.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb tense in each part. In a story told in the past, which verbs suddenly move into the present, and why? Check the first paragraph of Chapter 7.

languageFocusExercises.title: Say It Another Way
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say what Satan did and how Adam felt?

transformItems.source: He started to whisper to them day after day, trying to persuade both …
transformItems.frame: He started to whisper to them day after day, and he [blank] persuade both.

transformItems.source: As soon as Adam (pbuh) had finished eating, he felt his heart tighten and fill with pain, sadness, and shame.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A participle clause (“…, trying to persuade both”) adds an action that goes on at the same time as the main one; in full, it is “and he was trying to persuade both”. “As soon as + past perfect” and “No sooner + had + subject + past participle … than …” both show that one event follows another immediately. After “No sooner” at the start, the subject and auxiliary change places.

feedback.correct: Well done. You expanded the participle and used inversion correctly.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: show an action in progress. Item 2: after “No sooner”, put had before the subject, then the past participle.

languageFocusExercises.title: Condition, Possibility, Earlier Past
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct words for each sentence from Chapter 7.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which form fits Adam’s thoughts and what they forgot?

formChoices.sentence: Adam (pbuh) started to ask himself: “What will happen if I [choice] from this tree?
options: will eat
eat
ate

formChoices.sentence: It [choice] truly be the Tree of Immortality.”

has to
might

formChoices.sentence: They forgot that Allah [choice] them not to approach it and that Iblis was their bitter enemy.

has warned

languageFocusExercises.explanation: In a real (first) conditional, the if-clause uses the present simple, not “will”: “What will happen if I eat …?”. “Might” shows that Adam is not sure; “must” and “has to” would show certainty, which does not fit a man asking himself questions. The past perfect “had warned” places the warning before the moment they forgot it.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the forms for condition, uncertainty and the earlier past.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Is it an if-clause, is Adam sure or unsure, and which event happened first? Then check the second paragraph of Chapter 7.

languageFocusExercises.title: A Poor Choice

pages.title: The Realization & Repentance
pages.content:
“So he (Satan) made them (Adam (pbuh) and Eve) fall through deception. And when they tasted the tree, their nakedness became evident to them, and they began covering themselves with the leaves of the Garden. And their Lord called out to them, ‘Did I not forbid you from this tree, and say to you that Satan is a clear enemy to you?’” (A’raf: 22)

When they tasted the fruit, their private parts became visible to them. Adam (pbuh) discovered that he and his wife were unclad, so they both started cutting tree leaves in Paradise with which to cover themselves. They were in haste to hide their private parts because the sense of shame (haya) is inborn human nature and nakedness is contrary to human nature.

Adam (pbuh) bowed down, crying, “Forgiveness! Forgiveness!” so Allah asked, “Are you running away from Me?” Adam (pbuh) replied, “No, my Lord, but I am shy of You.”

After Adam (pbuh) and Eve were placed in Paradise, they enjoyed Allah’s blessings as they pleased. Allah warned them not to approach the forbidden tree. This tree is not described in the Holy Qur’an. It is only mentioned that Satan deceived Adam (pbuh) and Eve. According to Islamic scholars, this incident happened while Adam (pbuh) was in Paradise—that is, before he became a prophet.

vocabulary.definition: The act of making something false appear true.
Clearly visible or understandable.
Without clothing or covering.
Present in a person from birth rather than learned.
Not allowed by a clear command; here, the one tree Adam and Eve were told not to approach.

exercises.title: Why They Hurried
exercises.instructions: Choose the reason the writer gives in Chapter 8.
exercises.question: Why, according to the writer, were Adam and Eve in a hurry to cover themselves?
options: because the sense of shame (haya) is part of human nature
because Allah had called out to them
because they were afraid that Satan would see them
exercises.explanation: The second paragraph explains: “They were in haste to hide their private parts because the sense of shame (haya) is inborn human nature and nakedness is contrary to human nature.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer explains their haste with the inborn sense of shame (haya).
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of the second paragraph. Find the sentence with “in haste” and read what follows “because”.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Is Each Line Doing?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each line from Chapter 8 with what it does. The questions do not ask for new facts.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do the questions and answers do?

matchingPairs.left: Did I not forbid you from this tree, and say to you that Satan is a clear enemy to you?
matchingPairs.right: reminds them of a warning they already knew

matchingPairs.right: asks what Adam’s reaction means

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A negative question such as “Did I not …?” expects the answer “yes” and reminds the listener of something already known. “Are you running away …?” tests what an action means. The reply “No, …, but …” rejects one interpretation and replaces it. Repeating one word turns it into an urgent plea.

feedback.correct: Correct. You read each line for what it does, not only for what it says.
feedback.incorrect: Ask whether the speaker already knows the answer. Then look at the “No … but …” pattern in Adam’s reply in Chapter 8.

languageFocusExercises.title: Time, Result and Reason
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the narrator’s lines from Chapter 8 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words say when, what happened next, and why?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: [blank] they tasted the fruit, their private parts became visible to them. Adam (pbuh) discovered that he and his wife were unclad, [blank] they both started cutting tree leaves in Paradise with which to cover themselves. They were in haste to hide their private parts, [blank] the sense of shame (haya) is inborn human nature and nakedness is contrary to human nature.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “When” sets the time point that starts the chain. “So” introduces the result of the discovery: They began to cover themselves. “Because” gives the reason for their haste: shame is part of human nature. The chain moves time → result → reason.

feedback.correct: Correct. The paragraph now moves from time to result to reason.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each gap introduces: The moment something happened, what they did as a result, or why they hurried. Check the second paragraph of Chapter 8.

This tree is not described in the Holy Qur’an.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The writer marks the source of each claim. The quoted verse and the sentences “is not described …” and “It is only mentioned that …” report what the Qur’an contains and what it leaves out. “According to Islamic scholars” attributes the timing to scholars, and “that is, …” explains that same interpretation. A careful reader does not present the scholars’ view as words of the Qur’an.

feedback.correct: Correct. You kept the text separate from the interpretation.
feedback.incorrect: Look for source markers: A quotation, “not described in”, “only mentioned”, “According to …”. Which ones point to scholars? Check the last paragraph of Chapter 8.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Source-Aware Explanatory Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a fact you know from a source.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does the source say, and what does it not say?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response makes source responsibility visible, avoids turning interpretation into fact, and uses dialogue or rhetorical questioning for a clear discourse purpose.

feedback.correct: Keep the evidence hierarchy clear: Explicit source → unspecified detail → attributed interpretation → clarification.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what the source says: “The … says that …”
discussionPrompts.example: The official history of the Han dynasty says that a court official called Cai Lun presented a way of making paper to the emperor in the year 105.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what it does not tell us: “The source does not say …”
discussionPrompts.example: However, the source does not specify whether Cai Lun was the first person ever to make paper.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give someone’s view: “According to …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: According to many archaeologists, older pieces of paper have been found in China, so Cai Lun probably improved an existing method.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say it more clearly: “In other words, …”
discussionPrompts.example: In other words, he may have made paper better and more common, not necessarily invented it. Did he invent it, then? No, not with certainty, but he clearly played an important role.

pages.title: Repentance & Descent to Earth
pages.content:
Adam (pbuh) severely regretted what he had done. He immediately turned towards Allah. His regret itself was the reason for Allah’s mercy upon him. “They said, ‘Our Lord, we have done wrong to ourselves. Unless You forgive us, and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers.’” (A’raf: 23) Then Adam (pbuh) received words from his Lord (to learn how to ask for forgiveness), so His Lord pardoned him (accepted his repentance). Verily, He is the One Who forgives (accepts repentance), the Most Merciful. (Baqarah: 37) We said, “Go down from it (the Paradise), all of you. Yet whenever guidance comes to you from Me, then whoever follows My guidance—they have nothing to fear, nor shall they grieve.” (Baqarah: 38)

Allah taught Adam (pbuh) how to ask for forgiveness. This unintentional mistake committed by Adam (pbuh) was forgiven by Allah upon his repentance. This means that Allah did not abandon Adam (pbuh); He immediately turned towards Adam (pbuh), too. Adam (pbuh) and Eve left Paradise and descended upon Earth. At that time, there was neither a community nor a congregation. After a period of time following their descent to Earth, when a community emerged, Adam (pbuh) was given prophethood, thus becoming the first human, the first father, and the first prophet. We understand from the verses that humans are open to sinning and sometimes rebelling against their Lord. However, in order to remain an honored human, they must recognize their mistakes, seek the fault within themselves, and immediately turn towards Allah.

vocabulary.definition: Felt deep sorrow about a past action.
Compassion and forgiveness shown to someone.
Sincere sorrow for a wrong, together with a return to what is right.
The divinely appointed role of a prophet.
Regarded as having dignity and respected status.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Unless” Mean Here?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the prayer. Then choose the meaning of its second part.
languageFocusExercises.question: “They said, ‘Our Lord, we have done wrong to ourselves. Unless You forgive us, and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers.’” (A’raf: 23) What does the second part mean?
options: Even if You forgive us and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers.
Because You forgive us and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers.
If You forgive us and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers.
If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Unless” means “if … not”. It names the only thing that can prevent the result: without forgiveness and mercy, they will be among the losers. The prayer first admits the wrong (“we have done wrong to ourselves”) and then shows complete dependence on Allah’s forgiveness.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Unless” = “if … not”.
feedback.incorrect: Replace “unless” with “if … not” and read the prayer in Chapter 9 again. Which option has the same meaning?

languageFocusExercises.title: Why Adam Was Forgiven
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say why Allah forgave Adam?

transformItems.source: His regret itself was the reason for Allah’s mercy upon him.
transformItems.frame: Allah had mercy upon him [blank] his regret.

transformItems.source: This unintentional mistake committed by Adam (pbuh) was forgiven by Allah upon his repentance.
transformItems.frame: Allah forgave [blank] upon his repentance.
answers: this unintentional mistake committed by Adam (pbuh)
this unintentional mistake committed by Adam
this unintentional mistake that Adam (pbuh) committed
this unintentional mistake that Adam committed
this unintentional mistake which Adam (pbuh) committed
this unintentional mistake which Adam committed

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “X was the reason for Y” makes the cause the subject; “Y because of / due to X” puts the result first and the cause after a preposition. The passive “was forgiven by Allah” keeps the mistake as the topic; the active makes Allah the subject and the mistake the object. Both versions are correct; the chapter’s choices keep attention on Adam’s regret and on his mistake.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the cause and the agent clear.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: use a preposition of cause before a noun. Item 2: the whole noun phrase “this unintentional mistake …” becomes the object of “forgave”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Fix the Mistakes
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix these sentences from Chapter 9?

errorItems.sentence: Adam (pbuh) severely regretted what he has done.
options: have done

had done

must recognize

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The mistake came before the regret, so it needs the past perfect: “what he had done”. “Neither” is always paired with “nor”. A modal such as “must” is followed by the base verb without “to”; here one “must” controls three verbs: recognize, seek and turn.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the time, the negative pair and the modal verb.
feedback.incorrect: Check the tense for an earlier past action, the partner of “neither”, and the form of the verb after “must”. Then read Chapter 9 again.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what will happen if not: “Unless we …, we will …”

pages.title: The Settlement on Earth
pages.content:
Allah knew that Adam (pbuh) and Eve would eat of the tree and descend to Earth. He knew that Satan would violate their innocence. That experience was essential for their life on Earth; it was a cornerstone of their vicegerency. It was meant to teach Adam (pbuh), Eve, and their offspring the knowledge that Satan is their enemy and that the right path is to act in accordance with what they have heard from the Creator. The Creator is Knower, Powerful, Just, and Merciful.

Adam (pbuh)’s descending to Earth, then, did not imply dishonor or humiliation, but rather it was an honorable and respected settlement on Earth. And thus began the story of humankind and its struggle against Satan on Earth. There are many hadiths about the place of Adam (pbuh)’s descending upon Earth. Ibn Abbas, who narrated many hadiths, said: “Adam (pbuh) descended on land ‘Dihna’ between Mecca and Taif.”

It is also reported that Adam (pbuh) descended with the Black Stone (a large black stone set into the wall of the Ka’ba in Mecca. It is said to have come from Paradise).

Ibn Umar said that Adam (pbuh) descended on As-Safa and Eve on Al-Marwa (names of two mountains in the neighborhood of the Sacred House (Ka’ba) in Mecca. Part of the rites of pilgrimage (hajj) includes walking and running between these two hills in remembrance of Hagar’s search for water).

vocabulary.definition: A state of moral purity.
A basic part on which something depends.
Responsibility for stewardship and entrusted duties on Earth.
The experience of being stripped of dignity.
A religious journey to a spiritually important place.

hotspots.title: A Responsible Settlement

exercises.title: Who Reports It?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 10.
exercises.question: In Chapter 10, Ibn Abbas is the one who reports that Adam descended on As-Safa and Eve on Al-Marwa.
exercises.explanation: The chapter names two different sources. Ibn Abbas says Adam descended on the land “Dihna” between Mecca and Taif. It is Ibn Umar who “said that Adam (pbuh) descended on As-Safa and Eve on Al-Marwa”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The report about As-Safa and Al-Marwa comes from Ibn Umar; Ibn Abbas speaks about Dihna.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the reports at the end of the chapter. Check which name is attached to Dihna and which name is attached to As-Safa and Al-Marwa.

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Is the Source?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the reports from Chapter 10: is a person named as the source?
languageFocusExercises.question: Does it name who said it?

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “X said: …” and “X said that …” attribute a claim to a named narrator, in direct or reported speech. “It is reported that …” and “It is said to …” are impersonal passives: They pass on a report without naming who made it, and they keep some distance between the writer and the claim. When you summarise such a text, keep these frames; do not turn a reported detail into a plain fact.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated named sources from impersonal reports.
feedback.incorrect: Look for a person’s name before “said”. If there is no name, look for “It is reported” or “It is said”. Check the last three paragraphs of Chapter 10.

languageFocusExercises.title: The Future Seen from the Past
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the first sentence of Chapter 10. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Allah knew that Adam (pbuh) and Eve would eat of the tree and descend to Earth.” What does “would” show here?
options: something Adam and Eve used to do many times
an event that was still in the future at the time Allah knew it
an imagined situation that did not really happen
a polite request
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Would” is the past form of “will”. After a past verb such as “knew”, it looks forward from that past moment: at the time of Allah’s knowledge, eating from the tree and descending to Earth were still to come. This is called the future in the past.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Would” looks forward from a moment in the past.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: At the moment described by “knew”, had Adam and Eve already eaten from the tree? Then read the first paragraph of Chapter 10.

languageFocusExercises.title: Viewpoint, Purpose and Correction
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about the descent to Earth?

errorItems.sentence: He knew that Satan will violate their innocence.
options: violates
would violate
has violated

errorItems.sentence: It was meant to teaching Adam (pbuh), Eve, and their offspring the knowledge that Satan is their enemy …

After “did not”, use the base verb; the past is already shown by “did”. The last sentence uses “not X, but rather Y” to reject one interpretation and replace it with another.

pages.title: Adam (pbuh)’s Life on Earth
pages.content:
Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said: “The best of days on which the sun has risen is Friday. On this day Adam (pbuh) was created, and on this day he was sent down to Earth.” (see Muslim, Jumu‘ah 17, 18; also Tirmidhi, Jumu‘ah 1, 2; Nasa’i, Jumu‘ah 4, 45)

Adam (pbuh) knew he had said goodbye to peace, and he left Paradise. On Earth, he had to face conflict and struggle. No sooner had one ended than another began. He also had to work hard to keep himself alive. He had to protect himself with clothes and weapons and protect himself from the wild.

Above all, he had to struggle with the spirit of evil. Satan, the cause of his displacement from Paradise, continues to deceive him and his children. Satan wants human beings not to remember Allah, yet the removal of Allah from the human mind means the removal of meaning and purpose from human life.

The battle between good and evil is continuous, but those who follow Allah’s guidance should fear nothing, while those who disobey Allah and follow Iblis will be away from the mercy of Allah along with him. Adam (pbuh) understood all this, and with the knowledge of this suffering, he started his life on Earth.

The only thing that eased his grief was that he was master of the Earth and had to govern it. He had to maintain, cultivate, construct, and populate the Earth. He also had to reproduce and raise children who would change and improve the world.

vocabulary.definition: A serious struggle between opposing forces.
A sustained effort to overcome difficulty.
Direction toward the right course of action.
To prepare and use land for growing crops.
To establish or increase a population in a place.

hotspots.title: Struggle on Earth
hotspots.description: On Earth, Adam (pbuh) faced hard physical work and a constant struggle against evil.

hotspots.title: Building Human Life
hotspots.description: Adam (pbuh) had to cultivate, build and populate the Earth and raise children.

exercises.title: A Life Without Meaning
exercises.instructions: Choose the writer’s claim in Chapter 11.
exercises.question: According to the writer, what happens when Allah is removed from the human mind?
options: Human life loses its meaning and purpose.
People must work harder to keep themselves alive.
The battle between good and evil comes to an end.
Satan loses his power to deceive people.
exercises.explanation: The third paragraph says: “Satan wants human beings not to remember Allah, yet the removal of Allah from the human mind means the removal of meaning and purpose from human life.”

feedback.correct: Yes. For the writer, forgetting Allah takes away meaning and purpose; this is why Satan wants people to forget.
feedback.incorrect: Read the third paragraph again. Find the words “the removal of Allah from the human mind” and read to the end of that sentence.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reading “No Sooner … Than …”
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 11. Then choose the best meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: “On Earth, he had to face conflict and struggle. No sooner had one ended than another began.” What does the second sentence mean?
options: He faced one struggle at a time, with long periods of rest between them.
Each struggle was followed immediately by a new one.
A new struggle always began before the old one had ended.
He was able to end every struggle before it began.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “No sooner … than …” shows that the second event follows the first immediately. The inversion (“had one ended”) and the fronted negative make the sentence emphatic, so Adam’s life on Earth feels like a series of struggles without rest.

feedback.correct: Correct. The next struggle began as soon as one had ended.
feedback.incorrect: Did the first struggle end before the next one began? And was there time between them? Read the second paragraph of Chapter 11 again.

languageFocusExercises.title: Priority, Consequence and Contrast

pages.title: The Conflict of Habil and Qabil
pages.content:
One of their greatest joys on Earth came when Adam (pbuh) and Eve witnessed the birth of their first children. The children grew up to be strong and healthy young adults. Qabil cultivated the land while Habil raised cattle. In time, there arose a conflict between the two sons. Adam (pbuh) was in a difficult situation. He wanted peace and harmony in his family, so he prayed to Allah for help. Allah commanded that each son offer a sacrifice, and the one whose offering was accepted would be in the right. Habil offered his best cattle while Qabil offered his worst grain. Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted by Allah because of his insincerity in his offering. This angered Qabil even further. “I will kill you! I refuse to see you happy while I remain unhappy!”

The story of Habil and Qabil is narrated in the Holy Qur’an without mentioning names as follows: “Tell them in all truth the story of the two sons of Adam. When they made an offering and it was accepted from one of them and was not accepted from the other, the latter said: ‘I will surely kill you.’ Thereupon the former said: ‘Allah accepts offerings only from the God-fearing.’” (Ma’idah: 27)

The Qur’an narrates this story in a simple manner. It does not openly mention any of the details found in the Torah, as, according to the Qur’an, the only thing that needs to be known is the wisdom of the story. Habil and Qabil are referred to as Adam (pbuh)’s two sons without their names being given. Although we don’t know the whole story, Adam (pbuh)’s children, Habil and Qabil, were involved in a conflict that resulted in Qabil killing Habil.

A peaceful state in which people fit well together.
An offering given for a religious purpose.
Lack of genuine intention or honesty.

exercises.title: Two Offerings
exercises.instructions: Choose the reason given in Chapter 12.
exercises.question: Why, according to the chapter, was Qabil’s offering not accepted?
options: Adam had already decided that Habil was in the right.
Qabil was not sincere in his offering.
Grain was worth less than cattle.
Qabil had threatened his brother before the offering.
exercises.explanation: The first paragraph says: “Habil offered his best cattle while Qabil offered his worst grain. Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted by Allah because of his insincerity in his offering.” The threat comes after this because the result angered Qabil.

feedback.correct: Correct. The problem was Qabil’s insincerity, not the kind of offering: He gave his worst, while Habil gave his best.

languageFocusExercises.title: Why Start with the Sacrifice?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted by Allah because of his insincerity in his offering.” Why does the sentence begin with “Qabil’s sacrifice”?
options: because the writer does not know who did not accept the sacrifice
to keep attention on Qabil’s sacrifice and what happened to it, and then explain why
to show that this happened many times
to show that the writer doubts the report
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive puts the sacrifice, the topic of the paragraph, at the front, and “because of his insincerity” follows as the explanation. The agent is not hidden: “by Allah” is stated. So the passive here is about focus, not about an unknown doer or doubt.

feedback.correct: Correct. The passive keeps the focus on the sacrifice and its outcome.
feedback.incorrect: Notice that “by Allah” is in the sentence, so the doer is known. What, then, does the passive put first? Check the first paragraph of Chapter 12.

languageFocusExercises.title: Contrast and Omission in Other Words
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines about the two sons?

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “While” joins two contrasting actions in one sentence; in two sentences, the contrast moves to an adverb such as “on the other hand” or “by contrast”. “Without their names being given” is a passive -ing form after a preposition; the active version, “without giving their names”, needs a subject for “refers”, so the Qur’an becomes the subject.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the contrast and the omission.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: the blank sits inside the second sentence, so use a contrast adverb, not “while”. Item 2: after “without”, use an -ing form.

feedback.correct: Correct. You identified omission, comparison, attribution and admitted uncertainty.

pages.title: Habil’s Response & Human Moral Capacity
pages.content: Habil displayed his pious character in his response, saying: “Even if you raise your hand against me to kill, I will not raise my hand to kill you. Surely, I fear Allah, the Lord of the entire universe.” (Ma’idah: 28) It is understood from the above verses that although Qabil had the intention to kill, Habil did not adopt an aggressive attitude. Thus, he emphasizes that he does not take notice of the desires of his own self in the face of truth. At first glance, Qabil’s rebellious attitude may seem unacceptable. However, it is important to remember that humans have the potential for both good and evil. People can be jealous, selfish, greedy, and even damaging and harmful. The path to goodness is in controlling evil thoughts and actions and being moderate in desires. Thus, Allah tests us through our dual nature. Habil was intelligent, respectful, and always ready to obey the will of Allah. This contrasted sharply with his brother who was arrogant, selfish, and disobedient to his Lord. Habil did not fear his brother’s threats, but he also did not want his brother to be hurt. Allah gave Habil purity and compassion. Hoping to lessen the hatred in his brother, Habil said, “My brother, you are turning away from the right path and are sinful in your decisions. It is better that you repent to Allah and forget about your foolish threat. But if you do not, then I will leave the matter in the hands of Allah. You alone will bear the consequence of your sin.”

vocabulary.definition: Deeply committed to religious faith and conduct.
Ready to use hostility or force.

Kept within reasonable rather than extreme limits.

languageFocusExercises.title: Accepted First, Stressed Next
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort each pair from Chapter 13: the point accepted first, or the point stressed?
languageFocusExercises.question: Which point does the writer accept, and which does he stress?

dragDropGroups.group: A point accepted or mentioned first
items: although Qabil had the intention to kill
At first glance, Qabil’s rebellious attitude may seem unacceptable.
People can be jealous, selfish, greedy, and even damaging and harmful.

dragDropGroups.group: The point the writer stresses
items: Habil did not adopt an aggressive attitude
However, it is important to remember that humans have the potential for both good and evil.

A point accepted or mentioned first: although Qabil had the intention to kill
At first glance, Qabil’s rebellious attitude may seem unacceptable.

The point the writer stresses: Habil did not adopt an aggressive attitude
