languageFocusExercises.explanation: A concession admits a point without letting it become the main message. “Although” marks the conceded clause; the main clause carries the stress. “At first glance … may seem” presents a first impression, and “However, it is important to remember …” moves to the writer’s wider view. “People can be …” admits what humans are capable of, and the next sentence gives the writer’s answer: The path to goodness.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated what the writer admits from what the writer stresses.
feedback.incorrect: Look for concession signals (although, at first glance, may seem, can be) and for the part that answers them. Check the first half of Chapter 13.

languageFocusExercises.title: Concession and Hope in Other Words
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say what Habil did and why?

transformItems.source: It is understood from the above verses that although Qabil had the intention to kill, Habil did not adopt an aggressive attitude.

transformItems.source: Hoping to lessen the hatred in his brother, Habil said, …
transformItems.frame: Habil spoke to his brother [blank] lessen the hatred in him.
answers: in the hope that he could
in the hope that he might

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Although X, Y” concedes X inside one sentence; across two sentences, the concession moves to an adverb such as “However” or “Nevertheless” at the start of the second. “Hoping to …” is a participle clause that gives the speaker’s aim; it can be expanded into a clause of reason or purpose.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the concession and Habil’s aim.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: start the second sentence with a contrast adverb. Item 2: the blank must end just before the verb “lessen”, so finish it with “to” or a modal.

languageFocusExercises.title: Advice and Condition
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the verbs after “It is better that you”, “if” and “did not”?

errorItems.sentence: It is better that you repented to Allah and forget about your foolish threat.
options: will repent
repent
had repented

errorItems.sentence: But if you will not, then I will leave the matter in the hands of Allah.
options: would not
did not
do not

errorItems.sentence: Habil did not fear his brother’s threats, but he also did not wanted his brother to be hurt.
options: did not want
does not want
not wanted

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “It is better that you + base verb” gives advice; the second verb (“forget”) shows the same base form. In a real condition, the if-clause uses the present simple, even when the result is future: “if you do not, then I will …”. After “did not”, use the base verb.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the advice, the condition and the negative.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the verb with its partner: “repent … and forget” must match; an if-clause does not take “will”; “did not” takes the base verb. Check the end of Chapter 13.

languageFocusExercises.title: A Calm Answer
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about a conflict and a calm way to answer it.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response uses these resources to control viewpoint and logic: acknowledge tension, avoid overclaiming, explain intention, propose an alternative and make consequences explicit.

feedback.correct: Keep the modal claim genuinely possible rather than certain, and make the final condition follow logically from the advice.

pages.title: The First Murder & Burial
pages.content:
This brotherly request did nothing to lessen the hatred in Qabil’s heart, nor did he show fear of Allah’s punishment. Even familial considerations were given up. Qabil hit his brother with a stone, killing him instantly. This was the first death and the first criminal act committed by man on Earth.

Surah Ma’idah concludes the story with Qabil’s tragic end:

“At last his evil soul drove him (Qabil) to the murder of his brother, and he killed him, by which he himself became one of the losers.” (Ma’idah: 30)

When Habil had not appeared for some time, Adam (pbuh) began to search for him but found no trace of his beloved son. He asked Qabil about Habil’s location. Qabil arrogantly replied that he was not his brother’s keeper nor his protector. From these words, his father understood that Habil was dead, and Adam (pbuh) was filled with grief. Meanwhile, Qabil did not know what to do with his brother’s corpse. He carried it on his back, wandering from place to place trying to hide it.
His anger had now lessened, and his heart was burdened with guilt. He was getting tired under the burden of the corpse. It also started to have a stench. As a mercy, and to show that human dignity had to be preserved even after death, Allah sent two ravens that began fighting. At the end of the fight, one of the ravens died. The victorious bird used its beak and claws to dig a hole in the ground, rolled its victim into it, and covered it with sand.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to family relationships.
Relating to a serious unlawful act.
The body of a person who has died.
A sense of responsibility for wrongdoing.
Having won a contest or struggle.

exercises.title: After the Request
exercises.instructions: Put the events of Chapter 14 in order.
exercises.question: What happened after Habil’s brotherly request?

Qabil carries the body from place to place, trying to hide it.

The other raven digs a hole and covers the dead raven.

exercises.explanation: The chapter begins: “This brotherly request did nothing to lessen the hatred in Qabil’s heart.” Then Qabil kills his brother. Not knowing what to do, he carries the body and tries to hide it. Finally Allah sends two ravens; one dies, and the other buries it.

feedback.correct: Well done. The ravens appear only after Qabil has carried the body and does not know what to do.
feedback.incorrect: Follow Qabil through the chapter: The beginning (the request), the middle (what he does with the body) and the end (the ravens).

languageFocusExercises.title: A State Reached or a Process Going On?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Sort the parts of Chapter 14: a finished change, or one still going on?
languageFocusExercises.question: Has the change already happened, or is it still going on?

dragDropGroups.group: A state already reached
items: His anger had now lessened
his heart was burdened with guilt

dragDropGroups.group: Something going on or just beginning
items: He was getting tired under the burden of the corpse.
wandering from place to place trying to hide it
It also started to have a stench.

A state already reached: his heart was burdened with guilt
Something going on or just beginning: He was getting tired under the burden of the corpse.
wandering from place to place trying to hide it
It also started to have a stench.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The past perfect (“had now lessened”) and a passive state (“was burdened with”) describe a result that is already in place. “Was getting + adjective” shows a gradual change in progress, the -ing participles show ongoing actions, and “started to” marks a new process. Together they make the burden grow heavier step by step.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated finished changes from developing processes.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb forms: had + past participle, was + past participle, was getting, -ing, started to. Which ones describe change still happening? Check the last paragraph of Chapter 14.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build the Negative Chain
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tap the pieces to make the first sentence of Chapter 14.
languageFocusExercises.question: What word order comes after “nor”?
sentenceChunks: did nothing to lessen the hatred
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Nor” adds a second negative to a first one. When “nor” begins a clause, the auxiliary comes before the subject, as in a question: “nor did he show fear”. The sentence stacks two failed restraints: The brother’s request had no effect, and fear of punishment did not stop him either.

feedback.correct: Well done. After “nor”, the auxiliary “did” comes before the subject.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the request and what it did not do. Then add “nor” and use question word order. Check the first sentence of Chapter 14.

languageFocusExercises.title: After the Crime
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about Qabil after the crime?

errorItems.sentence: Even familial considerations were gave up.
options: were give up
were given up
gave up

errorItems.sentence: As a mercy, and to show that human dignity had to preserve even after death, Allah sent two ravens that began fighting.
options: had to be preserved
had to preserved
had to be preserve

errorItems.sentence: Qabil arrogantly replied that he is not his brother’s keeper nor his protector.
options: has been
will be
was

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive is be + past participle. “Familial considerations were given up” puts the lost restraint at the front, while the surrounding sentences keep Qabil’s responsibility clear. Human dignity does not preserve anything; it must be preserved, so the necessity form is “had to be preserved”. After a past reporting verb (“replied”), the reported verb usually moves back: “that he was not …”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected both passives and the reported verb.
feedback.incorrect: Ask whether the subject does the action or receives it, and check the tense after “replied”. Then read Chapter 14 again.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Consequence-and-Realisation Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone who ignores warnings until a problem grows.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the problem grow, and what helps in the end?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should use the target structures to organize discourse: Failed restraints → visible consequence → developing burden → purposeful learning moment.

feedback.correct: Keep the passive focused on information structure, make the developing state genuinely gradual, and ensure the purpose clause explains why the final example matters.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what was ignored: “He did not …, nor did he …”
discussionPrompts.example: Ali did not listen to his teacher’s reminder, nor did he read the message from his group about the deadline.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give the result: “… had not been started, and … was postponed.”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Show it growing: “… was getting bigger / becoming …”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say what the example showed: “… in order to … . It showed him …”

pages.title: Qabil’s Regret & Adam (pbuh)’s Advice
pages.content:
Qabil was in an extremely sorry state, as told in the Holy Qur’an: “Thereupon Allah sent a raven who began to dig at the earth to show him how he might cover the corpse of his brother. So seeing he cried: ‘Woe unto me! Was I unable even to be like this raven and find a way to cover the corpse of my brother?’ Then he became full of regret at his doing.” (Ma’idah: 31)

Witnessing this, Qabil was overcome with shame and guilt. “Woe unto me!” he exclaimed. “I was unable to do what this raven has done, that is to hide my brother’s corpse.” Qabil then buried his brother. This was also the first burial of man.

What is essentially being described here is the consequence of choosing evil. It arises from jealousy, which defeats the feelings of love and compassion of brotherhood. This story provides an example illustrating that with the guidance of revelation (wahy), choosing the truth over falsehood and goodness over evil will purify human nature of evil. In this example, Qabil represents the type of person dominated by evil, while Habil represents the righteous person who has love for goodness and kindness. Adam (pbuh) was in deep pain over the loss of his two sons. One was dead, the other was won over by Satan. Adam (pbuh) prayed for his son and turned to worldly matters because he had to work hard for his daily bread.

vocabulary.definition: To make something clean by removing what is bad or harmful.
Something untrue or opposed to truth.
A result produced by an action or decision.
Resentment caused by another person’s advantage or happiness.
Morally good and committed to what is right.

hotspots.title: Shame and Guilt
hotspots.description: Qabil was overcome with shame and guilt, and then he buried his brother.

exercises.title: Event or Interpretation?
exercises.instructions: Choose the sentence that is the writer’s interpretation.
exercises.question: Which sentence from Chapter 15 interprets the events instead of reporting them?
options: “Qabil then buried his brother.”
“This was also the first burial of man.”
“What is essentially being described here is the consequence of choosing evil.”
“Adam (pbuh) prayed for his son …”
exercises.explanation: The third paragraph starts a new step: After the events, the writer explains what they mean. “What is essentially being described here is the consequence of choosing evil.” The other sentences report what happened.

feedback.correct: Correct. This sentence steps back from the events and says what they show.
feedback.incorrect: Three of these sentences tell us what someone did or what happened. Look at the start of the third paragraph for a sentence that explains what the story “essentially” describes.

languageFocusExercises.title: Purpose and an Embedded “How”
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the verse quoted at the start of Chapter 15. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Thereupon Allah sent a raven who began to dig at the earth to show him how he might cover the corpse of his brother.” What do the words “how he might cover the corpse of his brother” describe?
options: the reason why Qabil had killed his brother
a question that the raven asked Qabil
a way of covering the body that Qabil did not yet know
the raven’s own reason for digging
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “To show him” gives the purpose of sending the raven. What is shown follows as an embedded how-clause: “how he might cover the corpse”, a method Qabil did not know. It uses statement word order, not question order, and “might” presents it as a possible way forward.

feedback.correct: Correct. The how-clause names the method that the raven showed.
feedback.incorrect: Read the words after “to show him”. What was Qabil unable to do, according to his own words that follow in Chapter 15?

languageFocusExercises.title: Say It in Full
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines about Qabil?

transformItems.source: Witnessing this, Qabil was overcome with shame and guilt.
transformItems.frame: [blank] this, Qabil was overcome with shame and guilt.

transformItems.source: … Qabil represents the type of person dominated by evil …
transformItems.frame: Qabil represents the type of person [blank] by evil.

transformItems.source: It arises from jealousy, which defeats the feelings of love and compassion of brotherhood.
transformItems.frame: It arises from jealousy. [blank] the feelings of love and compassion of brotherhood.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter packs information into compact forms. A participle clause (“Witnessing this, …”) can be expanded into a time clause. A past participle after a noun (“a person dominated by evil”) is a shortened passive relative clause (“who is dominated by evil”). A non-defining clause (“jealousy, which defeats …”) can be split into a second sentence, but the compact version links cause and effect more tightly.

feedback.correct: Well done. You expanded or split each compact form without changing its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: add a linker and a subject. Item 2: add who/that + is. Item 3: start a new sentence with a subject and a present simple verb.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The wh-cleft “What is essentially being described here is …” is a signal that the writer is stepping back from the events to say what they mean. After it, verbs such as “arises from” and “represents” present interpretation, not narration. The narrated events use the past simple.

feedback.correct: Correct. You found where narration ends and interpretation begins.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the frame “What is essentially being described here is …” and for verbs such as “represents”. Do they tell an event or explain its meaning? Check the third paragraph of Chapter 15.

languageFocusExercises.question: What happened, and what does it mean?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response describes what happened first, explicitly marks the move into interpretation, explains a cause or effect and contrasts two responses without confusing interpretation with fact.

feedback.correct: Keep event sentences factual and make the interpretive shift explicit.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what happened: “During …, …”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Compare two reactions: “While some …, he …”
discussionPrompts.example: While some players kept running to score a goal, he chose to help. One response looked at the scoreboard, while the other looked at the person.

pages.title: Adam (pbuh)’s Successor & Death
pages.content:
At the same time, he was a prophet advising his children and grandchildren, telling them about Allah and calling them to believe in Him. He told them about Iblis and warned them by telling them about his own experience with Satan and how Satan had tempted Qabil to kill his brother. Years and years passed, Adam (pbuh) grew old and his children spread all over the Earth. It was narrated that when Adam (pbuh)’s death drew near, he appointed his son Seth to be his successor and taught him the hours of the day and night with their appropriate acts of worship. Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) said: “Allah sent down 104 scrolls, of which 50 were sent down to Seth.”
Before his death, Adam (pbuh) told his children that Allah would not leave man alone on Earth, but would send His prophets to guide them. The prophets would have different names and miracles, but they would be united in one thing: The call to follow Allah’s straight path. This was Adam (pbuh)’s legacy to his children. Adam (pbuh) finished speaking and closed his eyes. Then the angels entered his room and surrounded him. When he recognized the Angel of Death among them, his heart filled with peace.

vocabulary.definition: A person who takes over another’s role.
Written texts on rolled sheets or similar material.
Persuaded someone to do wrong by making it seem attractive.
Guidance or influence passed to later generations.
Suitable or right for a particular time or situation.

hotspots.title: Seth Takes Over
hotspots.description: Adam (pbuh) appointed Seth as his successor and taught him the times of worship.

hotspots.title: Adam’s (pbuh) Legacy
hotspots.description: Adam (pbuh) left his children the call to follow Allah’s straight path.

exercises.title: Adam’s Last Years
exercises.instructions: Match each name with what Chapter 16 says about it.
exercises.question: What does the chapter tell us about the people and beings in Adam’s last years?

matchingPairs.left: Seth
matchingPairs.right: was made successor and learned the hours of worship

matchingPairs.left: Iblis
matchingPairs.right: Adam warned his children about him from his own experience

matchingPairs.left: The later prophets

correctAnswer.The later prophets: would have different names and miracles but one call
correctAnswer.The Angel of Death: when Adam recognized him, his heart filled with peace

exercises.explanation: Adam “told them about Iblis and warned them by telling them about his own experience”; he “appointed his son Seth to be his successor and taught him the hours of the day and night with their appropriate acts of worship”; the prophets “would have different names and miracles, but they would be united in one thing”; and “when he recognized the Angel of Death among them, his heart filled with peace.”

feedback.correct: Well done. You traced Adam’s warning, his successor, his promise about the prophets and his peaceful death.
feedback.incorrect: Iblis is in the first paragraph. Seth appears where Adam’s death “drew near”. The prophets and the Angel of Death are in the second paragraph.

languageFocusExercises.title: A Reported Detail
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence about Seth in Chapter 16. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: The words “It was narrated that …” present the detail about Seth as something passed on by others, not as the writer’s own direct claim.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “It was narrated that …” is an impersonal passive reporting frame. It attributes the detail to transmitted narration and keeps some distance between the writer and the claim. It does not say the report is false; it shows where the information comes from.

feedback.correct: Correct. The passive reporting frame marks the detail as a report.
feedback.incorrect: Who is the subject of “was narrated”? Is it the writer? Read the first paragraph of Chapter 16 again.

languageFocusExercises.title: Adam’s Advice
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about Adam’s advice to his children?

errorItems.sentence: At the same time, he was a prophet advising his children and grandchildren, telling them about Allah and to call them to believe in Him.
options: called
calling
to calling

errorItems.sentence: He told them about Iblis and warned them by tell them about his own experience with Satan …
options: by telling
by told
for tell

errorItems.sentence: … and how Satan had tempted Qabil killing his brother.
options: kill
for killing
to kill

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Items in a list should have the same form: advising …, telling …, and calling …, three actions of one prophet at the same time. After a preposition such as “by”, use the -ing form. “Tempt” follows the pattern tempt + person + to-infinitive.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the list parallel and used the right verb patterns.
feedback.incorrect: Check that the three actions in the list match, what follows “by”, and the pattern “tempt someone to …”. Then read the first paragraph of Chapter 16.

languageFocusExercises.title: From Reported to Direct Speech
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write Adam’s words as he might have said them. Write only the missing words.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happens to “would” when we use Adam’s own words?

transformItems.source: Before his death, Adam (pbuh) told his children that Allah would not leave man alone on Earth, but would send His prophets to guide them.
transformItems.frame: Adam (pbuh) said to his children, “Allah [blank] man alone on Earth, but will send His prophets to guide them.”

transformItems.source: The prophets would have different names and miracles, but they would be united in one thing: The call to follow Allah’s straight path.
transformItems.frame: “The prophets will have different names and miracles, but they [blank] in one thing.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: In reported speech after a past verb (“told”), Adam’s “will” becomes “would”. In direct speech it goes back to “will”. The two “but” clauses organize his message: Not abandonment but guidance, and different names and miracles but one shared call.

feedback.correct: Well done. You changed “would” back to “will” in direct speech.
feedback.incorrect: Direct speech uses Adam’s own time: His future is “will”. Keep “not” in the first item and the passive “be united” in the second.

languageFocusExercises.title: Write a Careful Legacy Paragraph
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about someone who passes something on to later generations.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does the person leave for the people after them?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should distinguish role from action, mark reported information explicitly, keep future events anchored to a past viewpoint, and use contrast to show how diversity can coexist with continuity.

feedback.correct: Keep each reporting frame attached to the claim it qualifies, and make the “would” forms consistently reflect the earlier viewpoint.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give their role: “… was …, collecting … and teaching …”
discussionPrompts.example: Mr Haddad was the founder of our town library, collecting old books and teaching children to read.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Report a fact: “It was reported that …”
discussionPrompts.example: It was reported in the local newspaper that he gave his own house to the library before he retired.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Look ahead: “He knew that they would …”
discussionPrompts.example: He knew that his former students would take over the library one day and that they would keep it open for everyone.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Show difference and unity: “… different in …, but united in …”
discussionPrompts.example: The librarians after him have been different in age and style, but united in one aim: To make reading free for all.

pages.title: The Challenge of Satan & Human Value
pages.content:
In Surah Hijr 39-42 Allah declares that for those who act in accordance with the Qur’an, Satan’s challenge has no meaning. Satan, too, acknowledges this fact.

“He (Satan) said, ‘My Lord, because You have put me in error, I will surely make (disobedience) attractive to them on earth, and I will mislead them all.’
‘Except for Your sincere servants among them.’
He (Allah) said, ‘This is a right way with Me.’
‘Over My servants you have no authority, except for the sinners who follow you.’”

Learning about Adam (pbuh)’s tale is to know the origin of humanity. Besides, to recognize Adam (pbuh) is to know the source of knowledge and the setting in which humanity came into being. The Holy Qur’an does not focus so much on Satan’s anti-God position. Although he is certainly a rebel against Allah and a symbol of disobedience, the Qur’an rather underlines his anti-human attitude and his constant attempts to tempt man away from his natural “straight” course. Satan alone is not strong; it is only man’s weakness and lack of morals and care that make Satan look so strong.
In fact, all the events that Adam (pbuh) and Eve experienced are like a summary of the adventures of their descendants in worldly life.
Each character in this Qur’anic story leaves behind a deterrent tale for humanity raising a key direct question: Where should man truly find his sense of value?

vocabulary.definition: To cause someone to follow a wrong idea or path.
Accepts or admits that something is true.
Power or right to control or influence.
A person who refuses to obey authority and fights against it.
The importance or worth given to someone.

hotspots.title: Satan’s Limited Authority
hotspots.description: Satan admits that he has no authority over Allah’s sincere servants.

hotspots.title: Where True Worth Lies
hotspots.description: The chapter asks where human beings should find their true sense of value.

exercises.title: Satan’s Real Strength
exercises.instructions: Choose the writer’s claim in Chapter 17.
exercises.question: According to the writer, what makes Satan look so strong?
options: his authority over every human being
his rebellion against Allah
the fire from which he was created
human weakness, lack of morals and lack of care
exercises.explanation: The writer says: “Satan alone is not strong; it is only man’s weakness and lack of morals and care that make Satan look so strong.” In the verses Allah says: “Over My servants you have no authority, except for the sinners who follow you.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer places the problem in human weakness, so people are responsible for their choices.
feedback.incorrect: Find the sentence that begins “Satan alone is not strong …”. What does the writer say makes him look strong? Check the verses, too: Does Satan have authority over everyone?

languageFocusExercises.title: A Claim and Its Limits
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each line from the verses in Chapter 17 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: Who can Satan mislead, and who not?

matchingPairs.left: I will mislead them all.
matchingPairs.right: Satan claims he will lead every person astray.

matchingPairs.left: Except for Your sincere servants among them.
matchingPairs.right: Satan admits that some people are beyond his reach.

matchingPairs.left: Over My servants you have no authority
matchingPairs.right: Allah denies Satan any power over those devoted to Him.

matchingPairs.left: except for the sinners who follow you.
matchingPairs.right: Only wrongdoers who choose his way come under his influence.

Satan claims he will lead every person astray.
correctAnswer.Except for Your sincere servants among t: Satan admits that some people are beyond his reach.
correctAnswer.Over My servants you have no authority: Allah denies Satan any power over those devoted to Him.
Only wrongdoers who choose his way come under his influence.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A broad statement (“them all”, “no authority”) is immediately narrowed by “except for …”. The first exception comes from Satan himself; the second comes from Allah. Together they show that Satan’s claim is not absolute: His influence depends on who chooses to follow him.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each broad claim and each exception with its meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Ask who is speaking in each line and whether the line makes a broad claim or removes a group from it. Read the verses in Chapter 17 again.

languageFocusExercises.title: Focus on the Real Cause
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say these lines from Chapter 17?

transformItems.source: Satan alone is not strong; it is only man’s weakness and lack of morals and care that make Satan look so strong.
transformItems.frame: What makes Satan look so strong [blank] man’s weakness and lack of morals and care.

transformItems.source: Learning about Adam (pbuh)’s tale is to know the origin of humanity.
transformItems.frame: [blank] about Adam (pbuh)’s tale, we come to know the origin of humanity.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “It is only X that makes Y …” (an it-cleft) and “What makes Y … is only X” (a wh-cleft) both put the real cause in focus and separate it from appearance: Satan only looks strong. “Learning … is to know …” equates two actions; “By learning …, we come to know …” shows the first as the means to the second.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the focus on the cause and the link between learning and knowing.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: a wh-cleft needs “is” before the focused cause; you can keep “only”. Item 2: use a preposition + -ing, or a clause with “we”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Keep What Is Conceded and What Is Stressed
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose the summary that keeps the writer’s view.
languageFocusExercises.question: “The Holy Qur’an does not focus so much on Satan’s anti-God position. Although he is certainly a rebel against Allah and a symbol of disobedience, the Qur’an rather underlines his anti-human attitude …” Which summary keeps this view?
options: The Qur’an does not present Satan as a rebel against Allah.
The writer is not sure whether Satan really rebelled against Allah.
Satan is certainly a rebel against Allah, but the Qur’an puts more emphasis on his hostility to human beings.
The Qur’an gives equal attention to Satan’s rebellion against Allah and to his hostility to humans.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The “although …” clause concedes a point with strong certainty (“certainly”). “Not so much … rather …” does not deny the first point; it moves the emphasis to Satan’s anti-human attitude. A good summary keeps both: What is accepted and what is stressed.

feedback.correct: Correct. The summary keeps the certain concession and the new emphasis.
feedback.incorrect: Notice “certainly” in the although-clause and “not so much … rather” around it. Is anything denied, or is the emphasis moved? Read the third paragraph of Chapter 17.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Qualified Final Argument
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say 8–10 sentences about something that seems strong but depends on us.
languageFocusExercises.question: What really gives it its power?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong B2 response should control scope, preserve a conceded point without losing the main emphasis, distinguish actual power from apparent power, and make the final question emerge logically from the preceding argument.

feedback.correct: Check that your exception truly narrows the broad statement and that your final question grows from the argument rather than appearing suddenly.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Make a claim with an exception: “Most …, except for …”
discussionPrompts.example: Most students find it hard to put their phones away during homework, except for those who keep their phones in another room.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Admit a point: “Although …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Although phone apps are designed to catch our attention, they cannot control our hands.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Name the real cause: “It is … that makes … look …”
discussionPrompts.example: In fact, the strongest factor is not the phone, but rather our habits. It is our tiredness and lack of a plan that make the phone look so powerful.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — End with an open question: “So the real question is: …?”
discussionPrompts.example: So the real question is this: What simple habit could help each of us decide when to use our phones?

options: a summary of their descendants’ life on earth
a dream that never happened
a story about a war

groupTask.title: Claims, Sources and Limits

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Answer eight questions to check your understanding of the key ideas across Adam’s story.

exercises.title: A Hidden Arrogance
exercises.instructions: Choose the best reading of the writer’s word choice in Chapter 5.
exercises.question: The writer calls Iblis’s arrogance “hidden” until Adam appeared. What does this word choice suggest?
options: Adam’s creation revealed an arrogance already inside Iblis.
Iblis became arrogant only after Adam was made from clay.
The angels also felt proud until Adam told them the names.
Iblis hid his arrogance from Allah but not from the angels.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “Satan’s—in other words, Iblis’—hidden arrogance came to the surface when Adam (pbuh) appeared on the scene.” The same paragraph says this arrogance “came from his belief that his origin was superior to Adam (pbuh)’s.”

feedback.correct: Well read. “Unapparent” means the arrogance was there but not yet visible; Adam’s appearance brought it “to the surface” rather than creating it.
feedback.incorrect: Look closely at “hidden” and “came to the surface” in the second paragraph of Chapter 5. Was the arrogance new, or was it already there?

exercises.title: Two Responses
exercises.instructions: Compare the two chapters and choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Compare Iblis’s words in Chapter 4 with Adam and Eve’s words in Chapter 9. What is the key difference?
options: Iblis asks for time to repent; they ask to stay in Paradise.
Iblis defends himself as better; they admit wronging themselves.
Both admit a mistake, but only Adam and Eve are forgiven.
Iblis blames his fire; Adam and Eve blame Satan’s whisper.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “I am better than he (Adam); You created me from fire, and You created him from clay.” Chapter 9: “Our Lord, we have done wrong to ourselves. Unless You forgive us, and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers.”

feedback.correct: Exactly. Iblis argues for his own superiority, while Adam and Eve look for the fault within themselves and turn to Allah. The book presents this as the way to remain an honored human.
feedback.incorrect: Find the words Iblis says at the end of Chapter 4 and the words Adam and Eve say in the first verse of Chapter 9. Who defends himself, and who blames himself?

exercises.title: The Slow Temptation
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 7.
exercises.question: Adam and Eve ate from the tree the first time Satan whispered to them.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “He started to whisper to them day after day, trying to persuade both.” Later: “Years went by, and Adam (pbuh) and Eve were preoccupied with thoughts of that tree. Then one day, they decided to eat of its fruit.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. Satan whispered “day after day”, and years passed before they decided to eat. The temptation worked slowly, through Adam’s forgetfulness and weakening determination.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the end of the first paragraph and the middle of the last paragraph of Chapter 7. How long did the whispering go on before they ate?

exercises.title: What the Experience Taught
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer supported by Chapter 10.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 10, what was the experience in Paradise meant to teach Adam, Eve and their offspring?
options: that the names alone are enough to guide every part of human life
that Paradise can be won back by working hard on the Earth
that Satan is their enemy and the Creator’s word is the right path
that angels and humans share exactly the same kind of knowledge
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10: “It was meant to teach Adam (pbuh), Eve, and their offspring the knowledge that Satan is their enemy and that the right path is to act in accordance with what they have heard from the Creator.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer calls the experience “a cornerstone of their vicegerency”: it taught who the enemy is and whose word to follow.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 10 again. Find the sentence that begins “It was meant to teach …”.

exercises.title: Adam’s Grief on Earth
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapter 11.
exercises.question: The writer says that nothing on Earth could ease Adam’s grief.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: “The only thing that eased his grief was that he was master of the Earth and had to govern it. He had to maintain, cultivate, construct, and populate the Earth.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. One thing eased his grief: His role as master of the Earth, with the duty to govern and build it.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the last paragraph of Chapter 11. The writer names one thing that eased Adam’s grief. What was it?

exercises.title: A Story Told Simply
exercises.instructions: Choose the reason the writer gives in Chapter 12.
exercises.question: Chapter 12 says the Qur’an tells the story of the two sons “in a simple manner”. What reason does the writer give?
options: The Torah had already given every detail of it.
The brothers’ names were not known at that time.
The killing was too painful to describe in full.
Only the wisdom of the story needs to be known.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12: “It does not openly mention any of the details found in the Torah, as, according to the Qur’an, the only thing that needs to be known is the wisdom of the story.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The Qur’an leaves out names and details because its aim is the lesson, not the full record of events.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 12. Find the word “as” after “details found in the Torah”: What reason follows it?

exercises.title: “At First Glance”
exercises.instructions: Choose the point the writer is making in Chapter 13.
exercises.question: The writer says Qabil’s attitude “may seem unacceptable” only “at first glance”. What point is the writer preparing?
options: Qabil’s anger was fair because his offering was refused.
Qabil was not responsible, since Satan controlled him.
Habil should have defended himself more strongly.
Every human can be jealous or selfish, so the test is ours too.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13: “At first glance, Qabil’s rebellious attitude may seem unacceptable. However, it is important to remember that humans have the potential for both good and evil.” And: “Thus, Allah tests us through our dual nature.”

feedback.correct: Well done. The writer does not excuse Qabil. He asks readers to see the same potential for evil in themselves because controlling it is everyone’s test.
feedback.incorrect: Read what comes right after “However” in the middle of Chapter 13. Is the writer excusing Qabil, or turning the lesson towards the reader?

exercises.title: The Real Rival
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to Chapters 1 and 17.
exercises.question: Chapters 1 and 17 both present Satan above all as an enemy of human beings, not only as a rebel against Allah.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “Satan is portrayed as a rebel against Allah’s command but also as a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) rather than Allah.” Chapter 17: the Qur’an “does not focus so much on Satan’s anti-God position” but “rather underlines his anti-human attitude”.

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The book opens and closes with the same idea: Satan did rebel, but his main target is the human being.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the last sentence of the first paragraph of Chapter 1 with the second paragraph of Chapter 17. Whom does Satan mainly oppose there?

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review the grammar, stance and discourse tools developed across the chapters.

exercises.title: Notice: Source, Report or Interpretation?
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences from the book into three groups by where each claim comes from.
exercises.question: Is it the Qur’an, a report from others, or the writer’s view?

dragDropGroups.group: What the Qur’an itself says or leaves out
items: The story of Adam (pbuh) is told in several chapters (surahs) of the Holy Qur’an.
This tree is not described in the Holy Qur’an.
Habil and Qabil are referred to as Adam (pbuh)’s two sons without their names being given.

dragDropGroups.group: A report passed on by others
items: It is also reported that Adam (pbuh) descended with the Black Stone …
It was narrated that when Adam (pbuh)’s death drew near, he appointed his son Seth to be his successor …
According to Islamic scholars, this incident happened while Adam (pbuh) was in Paradise …

dragDropGroups.group: The writer’s own interpretation
items: It clearly appears that human beings' earthly life is the scene of a division and contrast between good and evil …
The names refer to the fact that knowledge is the basis of science, technology, and culture.
In fact, all the events that Adam (pbuh) and Eve experienced are like a summary of the adventures of their descendants in worldly life.

What the Qur’an itself says or leaves ou: The story of Adam (pbuh) is told in several chapters (surahs) of the Holy Qur’an.
This tree is not described in the Holy Qur’an.
Habil and Qabil are referred to as Adam (pbuh)’s two sons without their names being given.
A report passed on by others: It is also reported that Adam (pbuh) descended with the Black Stone …
It was narrated that when Adam (pbuh)’s death drew near, he appointed his son Seth to be his successor …
According to Islamic scholars, this incident happened while Adam (pbuh) was in Paradise …
The writer’s own interpretation: It clearly appears that human beings' earthly life is the scene of a division and contrast between good and evil …
The names refer to the fact that knowledge is the basis of science, technology, and culture.
In fact, all the events that Adam (pbuh) and Eve experienced are like a summary of the adventures of their descendants in worldly life.

exercises.explanation: The book marks who is responsible for each claim. Sentences about the Qur’an (“is told in”, “is not described in”, “are referred to as … without”) say what the source contains or leaves out. Impersonal passives (“It is also reported that …”, “It was narrated that …”) and “According to …” pass on a report and keep some distance between the writer and the claim. Verbs of meaning and framing phrases (“It clearly appears that …”, “refer to the fact that …”, “In fact, …”) introduce the writer’s own reading. A careful B2 reader keeps these three levels apart when summarising.

feedback.correct: Well done. You separated the source, reported information and the writer’s interpretation.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the opening words of each sentence: Does it describe the Qur’an, pass on a report (reported, narrated, according to), or give the writer’s reading (appears, refer to, in fact)?

exercises.title: Notice: How Strong Is the Claim?
exercises.instructions: Read the three sentences. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 3: “… points to the breadth of Adam (pbuh)’s knowledge.” Chapter 7: “It might truly be the Tree of Immortality.” Chapter 13: “At first glance, Qabil’s rebellious attitude may seem unacceptable.” What do “points to”, “might” and “may seem” have in common here?
options: They pass on what another person said without naming the source.
They present a meaning as possible, indirect or a first impression, not as a settled fact.
They show that the speaker or writer believes the idea is false.
They describe something that happened regularly in the past.
exercises.explanation: All three lower the strength of a claim. “Points to” indicates a meaning without stating it fully; “shows” or “means” would be stronger. “Might” shows that Adam is not sure. “At first glance … may seem” offers a first impression that the writer can still qualify. None of them says the idea is false: They keep it open. B2 writers choose between shows / points to / may / might to match the strength of their evidence.

feedback.correct: Correct. These forms soften a claim; they do not reject it.
feedback.incorrect: Compare “points to” with “shows”, and “may seem” with “is”. Which version is more certain? Check Chapters 3, 7 and 13.

exercises.title: Notice: Contrast, Answer, Reframe
exercises.instructions: Match each part of the book with what the writer does.
exercises.question: How does the writer set ideas against each other?

matchingPairs.left: While Satan reached the point of no return by challenging his Creator, Adam (pbuh) took a path completely different from him.
matchingPairs.right: sets two opposite directions side by side

matchingPairs.left: He underlines his superiority because of the material from which he was created, yet Adam (pbuh)’s humble origin shows that Allah does not focus on origins
matchingPairs.right: answers a claim with evidence that works against it

matchingPairs.left: Adam (pbuh)’s tale is not symbolic or imaginary, but it is an original factual tale
matchingPairs.right: rejects one description and puts another in its place

matchingPairs.left: The Holy Qur’an does not focus so much on Satan’s anti-God position. … the Qur’an rather underlines his anti-human attitude
matchingPairs.right: keeps a first point but shifts the main emphasis to a second one

correctAnswer.While Satan reached the point of no retu: sets two opposite directions side by side
correctAnswer.He underlines his superiority because of: answers a claim with evidence that works against it
correctAnswer.Adam (pbuh)’s tale is not symbolic or im: rejects one description and puts another in its place
correctAnswer.The Holy Qur’an does not focus so much o: keeps a first point but shifts the main emphasis to a second one

exercises.explanation: “While” (= whereas) puts two contrasting actions in one sentence. “Yet” introduces evidence against the claim just made. “not + X, but + Y” rejects X completely and replaces it with Y. “not so much + X + but rather + Y” is softer: X is still accepted, but the emphasis moves to Y. Choosing the right frame keeps the writer’s exact stance.

feedback.correct: Correct. You told apart contrast, counter-evidence, rejection and a shift of emphasis.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each part: Are two sides compared, is a claim answered, is an idea rejected, or is an idea kept but made less important?

exercises.title: Build: Passive or Active?
exercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence so that the doer comes first. Write only the missing words.
exercises.question: What changes when the doer comes first?

transformItems.source: He was given the necessary spiritual, moral, mental, and psychological abilities.
transformItems.frame: Allah [blank] the necessary spiritual, moral, mental, and psychological abilities.

transformItems.source: After Adam (pbuh) and Eve were placed in Paradise, they enjoyed Allah’s blessings as they pleased.
transformItems.frame: After Allah [blank] in Paradise, they enjoyed Allah’s blessings as they pleased.

transformItems.source: Qabil’s sacrifice was not accepted by Allah because of his insincerity in his offering.
transformItems.frame: Allah [blank] because of his insincerity in his offering.
answers: did not accept the sacrifice of Qabil

exercises.explanation: In the active, the doer (Allah) becomes the subject, and the person or thing affected becomes the object. Both versions are correct, but they put different information first. The book uses the passive because its topic in each sentence is Adam, Adam and Eve, or Qabil’s sacrifice. The agent can be left out when it is obvious (“He was given …”) or added with “by” when it matters (“was not accepted by Allah”).

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved the doer to the front without changing the meaning.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Who gave, who placed, who did not accept? Put that doer first, then the verb in the past simple, then the object.

exercises.title: Build: Narrow, Concede, Turn
exercises.instructions: Complete the lines from the book with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word fits each gap?
exercises.fillBlanksText: … Satan is portrayed as a rebel against Allah’s command but also as a rival and enemy of Adam (pbuh) [blank] Allah. … [blank] we don’t know the whole story, Adam (pbuh)’s children, Habil and Qabil, were involved in a conflict … At first glance, Qabil’s rebellious attitude may seem unacceptable. [blank], it is important to remember that humans have the potential for both good and evil.
exercises.explanation: “Rather than” narrows the claim: Satan’s rival is Adam, not Allah. “Although” + a full clause concedes a gap in our knowledge before the writer states what is known. “However” at the start of a new sentence turns from a first impression (“may seem”) to the writer’s wider view. “Despite” cannot take a full clause: It needs a noun or an -ing form.

feedback.correct: Well done. You narrowed, conceded and turned the argument with the right linker.
feedback.incorrect: Look at what follows each gap: A noun (Allah), a full clause, or a new sentence after a first impression?

exercises.title: Build: Time Viewpoint and Claim Strength
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
exercises.question: Can you fix the time in two sentences and a claim that is too strong?

errorItems.sentence: Allah commanded that each son offer a sacrifice, and the one whose offering was accepted will be in the right.
options: would be
is
had been

errorItems.sentence: Adam (pbuh) knew he has said goodbye to peace, and he left Paradise.
options: says
had said
was saying

errorItems.sentence: We understand from the verses that humans are open to sinning and always rebelling against their Lord.
options: never
sometimes
constantly

exercises.explanation: From a past viewpoint, a later event takes “would”: when Allah gave the command, the result was still to come (Chapter 12). An event that happened before another past moment takes the past perfect: Adam had already said goodbye to peace when he knew it (Chapter 11). “Always” overclaims: Chapter 9 says humans are open to “sometimes” rebelling, a limited claim that leaves room for repentance. Check both the time viewpoint and the strength of every claim.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed two time forms and one overclaim.
feedback.incorrect: For each sentence ask: Is the event later or earlier than the past moment? Is the claim stronger than the chapter says? Check Chapters 9, 11 and 12.

exercises.title: Build: Naming the Cause
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct words for each sentence from the book.
exercises.question: Which word gives the cause in each sentence?

formChoices.sentence: So, in essence, people are from the same soil and they have no superiority over one another [choice] the difference in their colors.
options: because
due to
so

formChoices.sentence: His regret itself was the reason [choice] Allah’s mercy upon him.
options: of
why
for

formChoices.sentence: Satan alone is not strong; it is only man’s weakness and lack of morals and care [choice] make Satan look so strong.
options: what
that
who

exercises.explanation: “Due to” and “because of” are followed by a noun phrase; “because” needs a full clause with a verb. “The reason for + noun” names what the cause led to; “the reason why” needs a clause. “it is only + cause + that …” is an it-cleft: It puts the real cause in focus and separates it from appearance because Satan only looks strong.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each cause with the form that fits it.
feedback.incorrect: Look at what comes after the gap: A noun phrase, a noun after “the reason”, or a verb after “it is only …”?

exercises.title: Use: A New Screen at School
exercises.instructions: Complete this new paragraph with words from the bank. Three words are extra.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words to write about a change at school?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Last month, our school replaced the paper notices in the corridor with a digital screen. At first glance, the change may seem to be only about saving paper. [blank], the student council says that its real aim is to share news faster [blank] to save money. [blank] a short survey by the council, most students now read the notices every day, [blank] only sixty students answered it. So the screen [blank] be helping, but we cannot be sure until the council asks more students.
exercises.explanation: “However” turns from the first impression to the real aim. “Rather than” narrows the aim: Speed, not money. “According to” names the source of the evidence, and “although” concedes its limit: Only sixty answers. “Might” keeps the conclusion open; “must” would claim a certainty that the last clause (“we cannot be sure”) rejects.

feedback.correct: Well done. Your paragraph reports, reframes and qualifies like a careful writer.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap ask: A turn, a narrowed aim, a source, a limit, or a careful conclusion? Check what follows the gap.

exercises.title: Use: Say It More Carefully
exercises.instructions: Make each new sentence more careful. Write only the missing words.
exercises.question: Can you say these things more carefully?

transformItems.source: The new timetable is the reason for our better marks.
transformItems.frame: The new timetable [blank] one reason for our better marks.

transformItems.source: Some students say that the school trip has been cancelled, but nobody knows who said it first.
transformItems.frame: It [blank] that the school trip has been cancelled.

transformItems.source: Last week our coach said, “The team will win the next match.”
transformItems.frame: Last week our coach said that the team [blank] the next match.

exercises.explanation: “May / might / could be one reason” turns a certain cause into a possible one. “It is said / reported that …” passes on a claim without naming its source and keeps your distance from it. After a past reporting verb, “will” becomes “would”: the win was still in the future when the coach spoke.

feedback.correct: Well done. Your sentences claim only what the speaker knows.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: How sure is the speaker? Who said it? When was the prediction made?

exercises.title: Use: A Careful Argument
exercises.instructions: Write 6–8 sentences about a rule or change in your school or town. Plan with a partner first.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s language to argue for your view carefully?
exercises.explanation: Example: “Our school now asks students to leave their phones in a box during lessons. At first glance, this rule may seem unfair because phones can be useful for research. However, I believe it is a good rule. According to our class teacher, students ask more questions in lessons now. It is also reported that fewer phones are lost or broken. This could mean that the rule helps us concentrate, although it does not prove that everyone learns better. The real aim of the rule is not to punish us, but rather to protect our attention. So I would keep it, at least until we have clearer evidence.”

feedback.correct: Check your paragraph: A clear position; at first glance … may seem …, however …; according to … / it is reported that …; could / might; although …; not …, but rather …; a conclusion that stays inside your evidence.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Start with a first view: “At first glance, … may seem …. However, I believe …”
discussionPrompts.example: At first glance, the new rule to collect phones at the start of each lesson may seem too strict. However, I believe it is a fair rule for most classes.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Name your source: “According to …, …” / “It is reported that …”
discussionPrompts.example: According to our class survey, eighteen of twenty-five students check their phones during lessons. It is reported that a nearby school had better test results after a similar rule.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Stay careful: “This could mean that …, although it does not prove that …”
discussionPrompts.example: This could mean that the rule helps students concentrate, although it does not prove that phones were the only problem.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — End with your view: “The real aim is not …, but rather …. So I would …”
discussionPrompts.example: The real aim is not to punish students, but rather to protect learning time. So I would support the rule, at least until the end of the year, when we can look at the results again.

pages.title: Vocabulary Challenge
pages.content: Match key B2 words from the story with their meanings.

vocabularyPairs.meaning: Beyond ordinary natural processes through divine power.

vocabularyPairs.meaning: An organized society with developed culture and knowledge.
vocabularyPairs.context: The names taught to Adam (pbuh) could be the fundamental knowledge of being human, thinking, forming logical judgments, and producing civilization and culture.
Having such honor and privilege of knowledge required even the angels to prostrate themselves before Adam (pbuh).

vocabularyPairs.context: “And you, Adam, inhabit the Garden, you and your wife, and eat whatever you wish; but do not approach this tree, for fear that you become wrongdoers.”

vocabularyPairs.meaning: To make something clean by removing what is bad or harmful.

vocabularyPairs.context: This was Adam (pbuh)’s legacy to his children.

pages.title: Master Glossary
pages.content: Review the active Word Notes from all seventeen chapters.

vocabulary.storyExample: He was created from clay without parents, as a miraculous sign of Allah’s unlimited power.

vocabulary.definition: Remarkable or extraordinary in character.
vocabulary.storyExample: It also includes the Unseen (al-ghayb), and this makes the story fabulous.

vocabulary.definition: Concerned with basic questions of knowledge and existence.
vocabulary.storyExample: The tale gives us a unique and deeply philosophical understanding of life.

vocabulary.definition: The hidden reality that the human senses cannot perceive.
vocabulary.storyExample: It also includes the Unseen (al-ghayb), and this makes the story fabulous.

vocabulary.definition: A clear difference between opposing ideas.
vocabulary.storyExample: It clearly appears that human beings' earthly life is the scene of a division and contrast between good and evil as opposed to each other.

vocabulary.definition: The materials or elements that form something.
vocabulary.storyExample: These different expressions are used to describe both the composition and the various stages of mud, which is a mixture of water and soil.

vocabulary.definition: A whole formed by combining different substances.
vocabulary.storyExample: These different expressions are used to describe both the composition and the various stages of mud, which is a mixture of water and soil.

vocabulary.definition: The state of being regarded as higher or better.
vocabulary.storyExample: Therefore, from mankind we have white, red, black, and yellow ones; we have good and evil, ease and sorrow, and what comes in between them.” (see Abu Dawud, Sunnah 16; Tirmidhi, Tafsir 2/1) So, in essence, people are from the same soil and they have no superiority over one another due to the difference in their colors.

vocabulary.definition: A person from whom later generations descend.
vocabulary.storyExample: It is clear that Adam (pbuh) did not evolve from any other living being, but was created from the earth and was the first ancestor of a completely separate species of human being.

vocabulary.definition: A distinct biological group of living beings.
vocabulary.storyExample: It is clear that Adam (pbuh) did not evolve from any other living being, but was created from the earth and was the first ancestor of a completely separate species of human being.

vocabulary.definition: A person entrusted with responsibility on behalf of another.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Vicegerent & The Gift of Knowledge
vocabulary.storyExample: To be a representative, Adam (pbuh) needed some extraordinary qualities.

vocabulary.definition: Very unusual or remarkable.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Vicegerent & The Gift of Knowledge
vocabulary.storyExample: To be a representative, Adam (pbuh) needed some extraordinary qualities.

vocabulary.definition: Basic and essential to a larger structure.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Vicegerent & The Gift of Knowledge
vocabulary.storyExample: The names taught to Adam (pbuh) could be the fundamental knowledge of being human, thinking, forming logical judgments, and producing civilization and culture.

vocabulary.definition: An organized society with developed culture and knowledge.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Vicegerent & The Gift of Knowledge
vocabulary.storyExample: The names taught to Adam (pbuh) could be the fundamental knowledge of being human, thinking, forming logical judgments, and producing civilization and culture.

vocabulary.definition: The ability to learn, reason, and use knowledge.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: The Vicegerent & The Gift of Knowledge
vocabulary.storyExample: The knowledge that was given to Adam (pbuh) means the beginning of the skill for learning and speaking language and using intelligence.

vocabulary.definition: A person’s children and later descendants.
vocabulary.storyExample: The reason why Adam (pbuh) and his offspring are considered higher and more valuable than other beings (see Isra: 70) is because of the power of knowledge that Allah gave them.

vocabulary.definition: Divine knowledge communicated through prophets.
vocabulary.storyExample: However, in the Qur’an, Allah mentions another type of knowledge, which is the revelation (wahy) (see Nisa: 163-165).

vocabulary.definition: Absolutely necessary for an important purpose.
vocabulary.storyExample: One is necessary for mankind to maintain his worldly life, and revelation is essential to understand his role, duty, and the order established by Allah.

vocabulary.definition: A special honor or advantage.

vocabulary.storyExample: He refused, was arrogant, and was one of the disbelievers.’ (Baqarah: 34) ‘Except for Satan.

vocabulary.definition: The condition of being unable to do something.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Angels’ Prostration & Iblis’s Arrogance — Part II
vocabulary.storyExample: Angels admitted their inability and realized that Adam (pbuh) was the creature who knew what they did not know and that his capacity to learn was his most honorable quality.

vocabulary.definition: Willing compliance with a command or authority.
vocabulary.chapterTitle: Angels’ Prostration & Iblis’s Arrogance — Part II
vocabulary.storyExample: Angels’ prostration means obedience to Allah to show respect and admiration to Adam (pbuh) because the unique knowledge given to Adam (pbuh) is different from the knowledge of the angels that never changes.

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Complete the final challenge to demonstrate your mastery of Adam’s story.

exercises.title: Where Good and Evil Meet
exercises.instructions: Complete the writer’s sentence from Chapter 1 with one word: scene, cause, reward or end.
exercises.question: How does the writer picture human life on Earth at the start of the book?
exercises.fillBlanksText: It clearly appears that human beings’ earthly life is the [blank] of a division and contrast between good and evil as opposed to each other.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says: “It clearly appears that human beings' earthly life is the scene of a division and contrast between good and evil as opposed to each other.” Life on Earth is the stage on which good and evil face each other, and the rest of the book plays out this contrast.

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer presents earthly life as a stage where good and evil meet; Iblis, Adam, Habil and Qabil later act on that stage.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 1 again. Which word presents life on Earth as a place where something is played out?

exercises.title: From Honor to Earth
exercises.instructions: Put these turning points in the order the book tells them.
exercises.question: How does the book move from Adam’s honor to his life and mission on Earth?

sequencingItems.text: Adam bows down, crying “Forgiveness! Forgiveness!”, and tells his Lord that he is shy of Him.
Allah teaches Adam all the names, and Adam tells them to the angels.
After a community emerges on Earth, Adam is given prophethood.
Adam and Eve start covering themselves with the leaves of the Garden.
Adam and Eve leave Paradise and descend upon Earth.
Iblis refuses to bow down and claims that he is better than Adam.

exercises.explanation: Knowledge comes first (Chapter 3), then Iblis’s refusal (Chapter 4). After eating, Adam and Eve cover themselves and Adam cries for forgiveness (Chapter 8). Chapter 9 then says Adam and Eve “descended upon Earth”, and only “when a community emerged, Adam (pbuh) was given prophethood”. Chapter 8 also notes that the incident happened “before he became a prophet”.

feedback.correct: Yes. Note the last step: Adam’s prophethood comes on Earth, after the descent, not in Paradise.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the gift of knowledge in Chapter 3. For the last two steps, read the second paragraph of Chapter 9: what happens “after a period of time”?

exercises.title: An Unintentional Mistake
exercises.instructions: Choose the detail that best supports the writer’s description.
exercises.question: In Chapter 9 the writer calls Adam’s act “This unintentional mistake”. Which detail from Chapter 7 best supports this description?
options: They forgot Allah’s warning and that Iblis was their enemy.
Satan forced Adam to eat the fruit against his will.
Adam did not know that the tree was forbidden to them.
Eve picked the fruit first and offered it to Adam.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7 says: “They forgot that Allah had warned them not to approach it and that Iblis was their bitter enemy.” Adam knew the command (“Adam (pbuh) and Eve understood that they were forbidden”), Satan only whispered and persuaded, and it was Adam who “offered it to Eve”. The mistake came from forgetting, not from a deliberate challenge like Satan’s.

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer links the mistake to human forgetfulness, so he can call it unintentional while still showing that Adam knew the command.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the lines of Chapter 7 just before they eat. What does the writer say they had lost sight of?

exercises.title: Satan’s Methods
exercises.instructions: Match each statement by Satan with what it shows about how he works.
exercises.question: What does each of Satan’s statements reveal about his method?

matchingPairs.left: “I will come to them from before them, and from behind them, and from their right, and from their left”
matchingPairs.right: He will approach people from every side.

matchingPairs.left: “I am a sincere advisor to you.”
matchingPairs.right: He presents himself as a trusted friend.

matchingPairs.left: “Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree, lest you become angels, or become immortals.”
matchingPairs.right: He gives a false reason for Allah’s command.

matchingPairs.left: “I will surely make (disobedience) attractive to them on earth”
matchingPairs.right: He makes wrongdoing look beautiful.

correctAnswer.“I will come to them from before them, a: He will approach people from every side.
correctAnswer.“I am a sincere advisor to you.”: He presents himself as a trusted friend.
correctAnswer.“Your Lord has only forbidden you this t: He gives a false reason for Allah’s command.

exercises.explanation: In Chapter 6 Satan plans to come “from before them, and from behind them, and from their right, and from their left”. In Chapter 7 he swears “I am a sincere advisor to you” and claims the tree is forbidden only “lest you become angels, or become immortals”. In Chapter 17 he says “I will surely make (disobedience) attractive to them on earth”.

feedback.correct: Yes. Across three chapters the book shows one method: Approach from all sides, pose as a friend, give false reasons and make sin look attractive.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each sentence does: Which one describes directions, which one claims friendship, which one explains a command falsely, and which one decorates disobedience?

exercises.title: The Root of the Crime
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is supported by the book.
exercises.question: Chapter 15 traces Qabil’s crime back to jealousy, and his own words in Chapter 12 already show this jealousy.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 15 says the consequence of choosing evil “arises from jealousy, which defeats the feelings of love and compassion of brotherhood.” In Chapter 12 Qabil had already shouted: “I refuse to see you happy while I remain unhappy!”

feedback.correct: True. The writer’s interpretation in Chapter 15 is backed by Qabil’s own words in Chapter 12: he cannot bear his brother’s happiness.
feedback.incorrect: Compare Qabil’s angry words at the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 12 with the writer’s explanation in the last paragraph of Chapter 15.

exercises.title: The Path to Goodness
exercises.instructions: Complete the writer’s sentence from Chapter 13 with one word: moderate, sincere, humble or obedient.
exercises.question: According to the writer, what is the path to goodness for a human being who can do both good and evil?
exercises.fillBlanksText: The path to goodness is in controlling evil thoughts and actions and being [blank] in desires.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13 says: “The path to goodness is in controlling evil thoughts and actions and being moderate in desires.” The writer does not ask people to have no desires; he asks them to keep desires within limits, just as evil thoughts must be controlled.

feedback.correct: Yes. For the writer, goodness is not the absence of desire but control and balance because humans have “the potential for both good and evil”.
feedback.incorrect: Find the sentence in Chapter 13 that begins “The path to goodness”. Which word describes a balanced attitude towards desires?

exercises.title: Why the Ravens Came
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is supported by the book.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 14, the main purpose of the two ravens was to punish Qabil for the murder.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 14 gives two different reasons: “As a mercy, and to show that human dignity had to be preserved even after death, Allah sent two ravens that began fighting.” The ravens showed how a body should be covered, so even a murdered man’s body would be treated with dignity.

feedback.correct: Right. The writer names mercy and the dignity of the human body after death; punishment is not one of the reasons.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence in Chapter 14 that begins “As a mercy”. What two reasons does the writer give?

exercises.title: Two Sons Lost
exercises.instructions: Choose the reading the text supports.
exercises.question: Chapter 15 says Adam was in deep pain “over the loss of his two sons”, although only Habil died. How does the writer explain the second loss?
options: Qabil was later killed in revenge for his brother.
Qabil was won over by Satan, so he was lost in another way.
Qabil left the family and was never heard of again.
Qabil refused to bury his brother and was sent away.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 15 continues: “One was dead, the other was won over by Satan.” Habil was lost through death; Qabil, though alive, was lost to evil. The book never says Qabil was killed or sent away, and it says “Qabil then buried his brother.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The writer counts Qabil as a loss too: Alive, but won over by Satan.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence right after “the loss of his two sons” in Chapter 15. How is the second son described?

exercises.title: The Writer’s Key Phrases
exercises.instructions: Match each phrase from the book with what it describes.
exercises.question: The writer uses short, strong phrases to judge what he describes. What does each phrase refer to?

matchingPairs.left: “a humble material”
matchingPairs.right: the clay from which Adam was created

matchingPairs.left: “the point of no return”
matchingPairs.right: Satan’s challenge to his Creator

matchingPairs.left: “No sooner had one ended than another began.”
matchingPairs.right: the conflicts and struggles of life on Earth

matchingPairs.left: “Qabil’s tragic end”
matchingPairs.right: the murder that made Qabil one of the losers

correctAnswer.“a humble material”: the clay from which Adam was created
correctAnswer.“No sooner had one ended than another be: the conflicts and struggles of life on Earth
correctAnswer.“Qabil’s tragic end”: the murder that made Qabil one of the losers

exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “Allah created Adam (pbuh) out of clay, which is a humble material”. Chapter 6: “Satan reached the point of no return by challenging his Creator.” Chapter 11: “On Earth, he had to face conflict and struggle. No sooner had one ended than another began.” Chapter 14: “Surah Ma’idah concludes the story with Qabil’s tragic end”, the verse saying he “became one of the losers”.

feedback.correct: Yes. Each phrase carries a judgement: Adam’s origin is humble, Satan’s choice is final, life on Earth is an endless struggle, and Qabil’s choice ends in loss.
feedback.incorrect: Find each phrase in the book (Chapters 2, 6, 11 and 14) and read the sentence around it.

exercises.title: The Source of Human Value
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer the book supports.
exercises.question: The book closes with the question “Where should man truly find his sense of value?” Which answer do Chapters 4 and 5 already give?
options: In the material he was created from, as Iblis claims.
In his place in Paradise, which he later lost.
In his role as master of the Earth after the descent.
In the knowledge and capacity to learn Allah gave him.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4 says Adam and his offspring are “considered higher and more valuable than other beings” because of “the power of knowledge that Allah gave them”, and Chapter 5 says “his capacity to learn was his most honorable quality”. Origin is the answer the book rejects: “Allah does not focus on origins”.

feedback.correct: Yes. The book places human value in knowledge and the ability to learn, not in origin, place or power.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first sentence of Chapter 4 and the first sentence of Chapter 5. What do they name as the reason for Adam’s honor?
